I. SPEECH ON THE ANNIVERSARY OF LAURENCE, BISHOP OF MILAN.

How long will sluggish diffidence let me lie hidden in a narrow inner room? How long will excessive caution, overstepping the bounds of honourable fear, bring on the loss of reputation it is trying to avoid? For experience shows that among men, just as much of one's good name is stripped away by boldness, no less of it is lost, needlessly, through fear. A man should not be branded as one who grasps greedily at praise, nor be charged with a wish to make a show of feigned devotion, when he pays what modesty owes under the spur of love. Craving for glory, when it is pursued through speech, drives a man into the shadows; in the same way, failing to pay what you know is owed announces that night is near. To write what is superfluous is a matter of boasting; to keep silent about what is necessary is contempt. Often the praise of a teacher, when it is concealed, gives birth to reproach against ourselves. Someone may perhaps say, by way of advice, that a talent worn out and pressed by the size of the task withers into leanness, and that chatter which has lost the strength for speaking earns failure from the very abundance of its material: as if you were to pour the drop of a trickling eloquence into the bed of a great river, you would do nothing for its course by spending your liquid, and what is matched against the waves scarcely produces any moisture. But we reckon that what is said takes its value from the worth of the subject. A vein that is parched by nature often flows because of its theme; thin eloquence grows rich from what it sets out to treat. Often what is to be said is supplied by the merits of those to whom the speech has given itself, above all if the speaker serves in their praise out of pure affection: then affection furnishes an abundance of words; then love suggests what talent denies. As I am about to speak, so far as my modest powers allow, of the good deeds of Saint Laurence, I undertake a work full indeed of toil, but full of love. Away, then, with fear, the enemy of a reverent purpose! A mind subject to terror runs away from glory, as the apostle Paul cries out: "Perfect love casts out fear"; that is to say, and to show by a sure sign, he who trembles does not love. A man is overcome without blame by the immensity of a burden if, though unequal to carrying the load, he still comes forward devoutly. This being so, why should I not celebrate with a votive discourse the festival of the year now beginning? Why should I dishonour the opening of this bright anniversary with the ugliness of silence? Cheerfulness without speech is withered; to hide your joy is a semblance of mourning, and to have no voice in gladness is an imitation of grief. Shall I, then, holy father, conscious of my duty, not offer you words? Yet I wish to draw the beginning of my speech on your consecration from the season, and, if I can, to blossom in speech together with the flowery infancy of the reborn year: now, when the sap of the earth runs through the veins of dry shrubs into buds, and the belly of the dry tinder swells with moisture [?]; when in the gentle light the leafy tresses of the new growth unfold and all the interweaving of the branches spreads out, and the beauties of the leaves, which nature had confined within their sheath, are set free; when the song of the birds is adorned with tuneful sweetness; when the life of the crops, buried under the winter clods, is released as if from the bars of the cold and, warmed by the heat, is conceived; now, when the farmer measures his hope of fruit in the white blossom; when the sunny beauty of the vineyards is woven by the intertwining arms of the vine-shoots, and cultivation shapes a fruitful face before the time of ripeness, giving grace with the taming pruning-hook and checking barren luxuriance with the iron that brings forth fruit; when the fury of the deep sea passes into a gentle whisper and the ferocity of the winds, weakened by the warmth, turns into the sailor's delight; when it is safe to launch the boat upon the sea and release the anchors' bite, while the breaking of the storms that until now terrified sailors invites them and lets the helmsman sleep across the wet expanses of the sea; when the meadows, picked out in jewelled colours, grow rich with the wealth of spring, and the elements bear witness to nature's joy at the ordination of the high priest. Shall I not now render to you, bishop, what I have already learned to give to others? Gravity, modesty, chastity and grace brought you to the height of the episcopate; with so many gifts gathered together as into a heap you took up the venerable dignity of your present office, possessing the ornaments of so many virtues that each kind on its own would make a proven priest. I say nothing of the unanimity of all in your election, and I do not rehearse the concordant judgment of different nations: let these things stand in place of praise for one who has nothing to proclaim about character. For popular favour is generally driven by the shifting moments of uncertain goodwill, and the crowd of citizens, knowing nothing of careful examination, loves the unknown while it is carried away by partisanship. In your case, whoever made himself either partner or sponsor of your candidacy held the scales. The gathering of the unlearned multitude weighed your merit in the balance of the perfect; and while the variety of your adornments pleased them, as though you were the single heir of the most diverse training, each one judged that what he himself approved was enough for your distinction, since all your good qualities could not be known to everyone, and you had drawn them all, one by one, to the favour of your star: showing one that you are devout, another that you are stern, another that you distribute a well-gotten inheritance, another that you know how to keep what was rightly acquired. So the whole body took up this eagerness, that each, though he prevailed with the praise he had put forward, was yet outdone in comparison by another who had a better claim in your praises.

I do not wish to linger longer on these things. I must come to the trials of your labours, since I, who am not equal to the greatest things in praising you, do not know how to be content with small ones. While you were still unsteady in the new footsteps of the dignity laid upon you, the adversity of an inescapable time received you, and wars waged against liberty made the recruit of the episcopate a most practised soldier. You did not know how to fear the savagery of the brigand; with the shield of constancy you spat out the poisons of flattery, which among the malicious is the more harmful weapon. How often did he who could not overcome you in combat assail you with treacherous honours? How often, to the cost of your good name, did he believe that you would accept the pretences of his service, asking you to make a collusive pact, shut the enemy inside the city walls and hand over the limbs of your sheep to be torn apart by wolves, putting before you the examples of many who had done the same, which is a crime even to speak of? You despised all this as something to be shunned, and, keeping it for vengeance in a calmer time, you committed it to memory, retaining these detestable things lest they pass unpunished through forgetfulness, and feeling the greater horror at such excesses because you feared the ruin of others. But setting aside what hinders my speech, let us come to things more worthy of religious remembrance. When the hostile invasion scattered the Christian people in every direction like cattle, you were made captive in all of them by tortures of every kind; gathered up in fatherly love, you bore the torments of many, as the apostle says: "Who among you is tormented, and I am not?" Yet amid all this adversity never saw you broken. The enemy felt this much plucked from his triumphs: that he did not subdue the spirit of the captive bishop. You still fought for the release of very many, and, fearing nothing for yourself, you made known your anxiety for your people. I do not wish to dwell longer on sad things, nor to unfold the tragedy of an evil time; touching lightly on a few things from your illustrious way of life, I pass on, lest in telling of you I force you to endure once more what you suffered — although the teacher of the Gentiles recalls that he was trained in tribulation, crying out: "When I am weak, then I am strong." I say nothing of hunger, cold, injuries, and the aggravations of illness that the enemy's mind contrived for you. But, I suppose, these were trifles, and limbs made robust by the vigour of former health endured them! Was it not rather that, when your limbs were weakened in their joints and long since drawn away from their own strength by age, your soul alone, which did not know how to bend, sustained you, and, fixed upon the wall of constancy, fought against your assailants with a resolve worthy of imitation? After this Christ our Redeemer, who never disregards pious prayers, came to restore the longed-for state of liberty and made firm the broken strength of the Roman name with his skilful healing: the shattered state returned to wholesome vigour. When the heavenly Ruler looked down from on high with kindly eyes, the light of its own bishop was restored to the city of the Milanese. At that time inhabitants were few; there was aimless wandering in the houses and confused running to and fro across the dear thresholds of bedrooms; everywhere there was fear and grief, and the temples of God lay filthy, given over as lairs for wild beasts; wasting neglect had clouded once most splendid halls with the mould of long damp. You gave joy to others by your return; you yourself returned to tears. Then, like birds when the earth is clothed in snow and some small patch of ground is laid bare [?] in hope of food, you might have seen whatever remnants of the people had been able to survive flocking together, and flocks hurrying from every side to the presence of the good shepherd, while the woods grew weary with their bleating. Some you comforted with words and manifold kinds of support, others you refreshed at your own expense, others you encouraged by your example. Shortly afterwards the city, already buried, recovered its former state, which it owes to you after God, and the city, which did not believe that what it had been could ever be restored in it, began now to strive after better things. Then — such is the way of life — one could see everything drawn on by good success to broader progress.

I run through the particulars, relating briefly things that call for a long narration, so as to arrive at the great contest of your life, at the crowning glory of your purpose. Next, after a time of uncertainty, a second captivity arose in the Roman church, which was to draw you, as if you had long been idle and shy of toil, from the bosom of a long repose, when the weapons of your labour, scarcely laid down in the hope of peace, were taken up again. Silence would indeed be owed in so lamentable a matter, so that an abominable deed might perish from memory within a single generation, were I not drawn on by the duty of praising you. There the senate of the heavenly court was summoned; there a crowd of bishops gathered from various provinces, and that assembly brought as many varieties of opinion as there were kinds of men. But those in whom there was the spiritual savour of understanding held you, out of love, as leader of the chief deliberation. How you then tamed the onslaught of threatening men with the honey of gentle words, how you broke the hearts of the proud by raising up a venerable humility, how you grounded the minds of the wavering with the root of counsel, I cannot explain. Anyone eager to know what was done I send to the contemplation of the deed itself. So many chosen men followed you alone, and the leaders of so many great cities came round to your opinion. He who formerly broke away in raw obstinacy is now seething in the heat of lamentation, and he who is cut off has nothing for consolation but tears over his calamity. Perhaps some malicious interpreter of events will say: what decision did the present cause obtain from such constancy? Let him ask what came of this much-praised toil. To him I will confidently reply: under your presidency it was brought about that alien fury did not receive bishops as its servants, and that the judgment of bishops did not serve the indignation of those rushing headlong, lest the ill-disposed should take it as a precedent that what they wanted could come about. Finally, let the chatter of the wicked fall silent, at least out of regard for this hidden truth: that the fires of hatred, which blazed not from the guilt of the one attacked but from the kindling of factions, could not be quenched even by the fountain of holy deliberation. To you, therefore, is owed the safekeeping of the venerable canons; to you it is owed that whatever wickedness now rages has happened without the stain of the bishops; to you was laid bare what the accusers had woven before others with secret fraud; by you it was established that hatred must not be gratified whenever good faith abandons the assailant. But these things are better kept for telling at another time. Hail, star of the churches! As an emulator of Abraham, go on to a good old age, since it is a testimony of uprightness for a man to be preserved long in the citadel of the church, as it is written: "Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days." You, ripe in years yet youthful for religious toil, prevail; by your praiseworthy piety set examples before good disciples, restrain the wicked with severity, and, fastened by the clasp of both good works, endure without stain as a witness to the highest glory.
II. SPEECH SENT TO HONORATUS, BISHOP OF NOVARA, FOR THE DEDICATION OF THE BASILICA OF THE APOSTLES, ON THE SITE OF A FORMER TEMPLE OF IDOLS.

I believe, dearest brothers, that you revere with all the care of your minds the fact that in this place, while the name of temple remains, the old worship has perished in favour of true religion; that the reverence of a shrine has been established now that the libations have been driven out; that it is rightly called a sanctuary, since it has renounced its former victims and, by the change in the sacrifice offered, has taken the name of a house of God; and finally that the foundations have passed into another state while the roof stands unshaken, and, though human labour has added little to the structure, whatever was there has been renewed while remaining wholly intact. How great a miracle must we reckon it, that a building, while keeping its measure, still does not cease to rise, and, set upon ancient footings, is raised up by growth? We must surely ask who was the author of this work, of this renewal. It was, of course, the venerable bishop Victor, predecessor of my lowliness, upon whom God bestowed a name that foretold his future innocence. For whoever has come to the outcome foretold for the struggles undertaken against worldly vices — once you have learned his name, you know his deeds. Through spiritual combat, as befitted a victor, he triumphed over sins; and whatever the sinister side lays upon mortals, do not look for any fall from it in him, since you understand that he was what he was named. His merits call for a broad field of oratory, if the leanness of my talent or of my merit allowed me to range more widely; for there is a certain nobility in one's deeds in being found worthy of the praise of the great. While our lowliness follows him in the care of building, it has, with God's favour, brought his wishes to completion. Let no one think what I have said arrogant: it is right to join one's wishes to those of a man whom one cannot equal in action, since it is a sign of a good conscience to follow the better man in any respect. One never, I think, runs onto a dark path if one follows him whom one knows to hold out the light of life. Yet let us set out more plainly, by the service of speech, the truth of what was done. Here, formerly, the men of old worshipped images dedicated by deceitful sorceries and drenched with the foul blood of cattle; here, to the insult of God, upon an altar heaped with ill-omened offerings, they offered to demons the things owed to heaven; here the entrails of heifers, quivering with half-living movements, sang the future to the wretched inquirer; from here smoke, scattered with filthy contagion in many directions, polluted the very air. Finally, from here the multitude of victims slaughtered by butchers drove away whatever is God, while spelt, blood, incense and wethers were offered to idols, while an age hostile to Christ would not accept a simple rite and, as its wealth laboured under manifold offerings, purchased the displeasure of heaven. I would gladly go through the details and unlock with the key of the tongue the secrets of those deadly deeds, did we not rightly judge it an injury to the mouth to narrate foul things, and fear that what struck them down in the doing might defile us in the telling. Let us explain meanwhile by what blessings these things were changed, and with what splendour the night was overtaken and put to flight. Where are the figures of the deities, fashioned to the wishes of their makers, whose faces depended on the power of the craftsman, whose value was produced either by the worker's care or by the metal? Where are the gods to whom men gave power by the glitter of gems? Behold, I see that all these have fled, now, I believe, that Christ has entered. Let us consider by whose help he is supported. With him came the rays of heaven, the diadems of the apostles, Peter and Paul. For who would be needed in the restoration of a house but the architect and the rock? But the stone and the one who builds upon it? But the foundation and the craftsman? Why do you tremble, you perils of mortals? Why do you make ready to flee in anxious haste? He it is from whom no escape can hide your cunning, who, though he does not move from his place, follows you wherever you go. Come then, most loving Lord, and enter in fullness to consecrate your work; come, and through baptism of the human heart let these temples, hitherto dedicated to a foul patronage, be cleansed. Establish, Lord, by transforming them, the sacrifices, and while we heap the holy altars with pure gifts, make the presence of your majesty felt among us, summoned by the merit of holy priests, and above all by the conscience of our father Laurence, here present, who has raised the heights of the church with as many gifts as would each on its own make a supreme bishop; in whom flourish modesty, the chief of good works and mother of honour, patience, the nurse of holy religion, and piety that will always appease God; who has given the members of the church instruction for life not by words but by examples; who, going before, shows every path by which one goes to God; with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns with the Father for ever and ever. Amen.
III. SPEECH GIVEN TO STEPHEN, THE RESPECTABLE VICAR, TO BE DELIVERED TO BISHOP MAXIMUS.

A mind devoted to the praises of bishops reveals the vow of a religious conscience: it is a sign of good sense to dedicate our words to those who obey God. In praising them a cramped speech may perhaps reveal inexperience, but if one holds back, it shows mere speechlessness. Who would think a narration beggarly when devotion enriches it? Often, amid the gifts of eloquence, the vein of the eulogist is found poor, while on the other hand the treasure of the heart shines out through poverty of words. He who judges in God's stead does not desire painted discourse, but that which an unvarnished brightness of mind commends; for in the one, eloquence flatters even without love, while in the other, naked truth commends its own splendour. Everything that affection dictates is without trappings; it is the things we wish to have not so much the reality of the right as its likeness that are fashioned to a nicety. My speech is addressed to you, my venerable bishop Maximus, in whom virtue, bearing witness to your merits, began with your name, and in whom your conduct proclaims what your name declares. The foresight of your parents wished you to be chosen before you were proved. Long ago, when you were engaged in secular offices, the toil of the camp trained you, and adversity made you firm for the government of the church, as God says through the prophet: "He who is faithful in little is faithful also in much." The judge of sacred affairs [?] earned you as companion both in counsel and in labour. Rightly were you to be consecrated at the venerable altars, for even in lay life you chose what was sacred. You were found a guardian of chastity at an age when even the law gives way to desire; it is enough to shudder at the pursuits of youth that licence supports. Christ seeks among the enemy's ranks the soldiers whom he will raise to the rank of commander. Once admitted to the church, you fulfilled the part of a bishop in your deeds before the time of your dignity. Your kindness was no stranger to you: resting on the roots of nature, it showed the bud from the white blossom. Everything that is feigned is temporary; what ripens with age is lasting. We do not believe that the priesthood came to you as a gift, but as a reward. Others are commended by the breeze of popular favour, with goodwill acting as go-between; to you strict severity toward the guilty won affection. You possess a singular wisdom, which, though desirable in everyone, is necessary in a teacher. In vain does a man take on the role of admonisher if he cannot weigh the burden of the office laid upon him; he who is higher in honour is to be ranked with the lowest unless he excels in knowledge. It was judgment, not favour, that gave you your high place. Worthy of a bishop is the love that discernment wins; he mars the dignity of a teacher who wishes to please by favour alone. Taught and shaped by these gifts of heaven, you instruct the people more by doing than by speaking. Admonitions offered by example clear away every pretext from disciples; he who has not himself pursued innocence invites others to it shamelessly. Those who intend to sin fear you as a witness even in the secret depths of their rooms: fear and reverence for you keep faults from taking effect as they arise. He who confronts vices at their beginnings both removes the occasion of falling and purges the source of desire. I have dedicated these few words to your beatitude, briefly as it were, to commend my tongue to you. If success in life smiles on your prayers, I will devote myself to a full account of your deeds, so that what is known to all may be preserved in writings that will endure for posterity, for the joy of the age to come.
IV. SPEECH FOR A DEDICATION, SENT TO BISHOP MAXIMUS.

A poor vein of talent need never be feared when the occasion for speaking is rich. Whenever our mind serves in heavenly worship, it rises above the merely human, and thinness of expression is not reduced to straits if the speaker renders homage to his Maker. For he who bestowed the tongue can adorn it with the gifts of eloquence, and he whom we confess to have given speech can give spirit to words. Long ago he came to the aid of a meagre prophetic speech, when the feeble speechlessness of Moses was raised up to the perfect eloquence of a teacher and to the trumpet-voice of a most mighty admonisher. Moses did not blossom by gradual stages as he practised his skill, nor did he climb to the harvest of perfection through the experience of any length of years. Though he had only a common soldier's untrained wit, when he was commanded to take up the office of leader he fulfilled it steadfastly, precisely because he had modestly declined it. So we too, as we celebrate this feast of dedication, wait amid the blessings of spiritual joy for grace, while we obey. Away with feeble fear; away with confidence vainly gained through study. With respect to the pattern of human perfection we neither presume anything nor fear anything. And then, who would hesitate to loosen even mute lips in praise of blessed John the prophet and of the apostle, whose entrance has sanctified this temple? The prophet's grace was older than his nature: since he had fulfilled the office of a holy seer before he entered the light, he marked the very threshold of this life with power. For at one and the same moment he made his mother renowned for fruitfulness and stirred his father's idle lips to their former speech, as the use of it returned. After the wonders of this earlier example, let no one who names John suspect that he will keep his former clumsiness of tongue. After most holy Zechariah, to whose throat the banished power of human speech returned through that very name, John the apostle is rightly believed by all to be the key of words. In his company Antoninus, a hero of an ancient age, and the glory of most blessed Cassian joined with him make of this building a holy mystery, of an earthly dwelling a heavenly fellowship, and of things made by hand something that no old age can violate. For things offered to God know no decline, and what is propped up by piety is not sent off into trembling decay. The solid structure that Christ enters stands firm, and, forgetting its original frailty, it acquires strength from its owner. Humble roofs are adorned by the nobility of the one who consecrates them, since a perishable thing is granted to take its worth from its lord. And you, most holy brother, who have offered this building, rejoice in the repayment of your reward. Hope cannot waver when it is promised the fruit of a good deed. Confidence in recompense springs from practice, and whoever devotes himself to praiseworthy things does not totter through any uncertainty.
V. ADDRESS OF A BISHOP AT THE START OF HIS OFFICE

A master who is just beginning is indeed the equal of his disciples, and a teacher at the outset stands in no higher rank than his hearers. Honour is owed to talents that have been tested; the untried can scarcely claim even modest [?] regard. True commendations are those drawn forth by long sweat. Whenever glory is heaped on someone before he has laboured, it is flattery, not judgement. Let a soldier count among his blemishes whatever triumphs he wins before the trial of the battlefield. Those who hurry into the Olympic contests: do they have any hope of the crown before the contest is over? For the apostle says, "No one is crowned unless he has competed according to the rules." See, praise before merit does not befit even those who may rightly claim it after their labour. Our condition, by contrast, lies a long road apart, for as much is plucked from the harvest of our innocence as is added from our labour. As I judge it, placed as I am in my apprenticeship, the road is full of constraint and danger: on it a praiseworthy life must be pursued, and yet that life becomes rich in disgrace if it desires to be praised by men. If our conduct grows proud of its own good works, it will be defiled, as the divine words testify: "Those who praise you lead you astray and overturn the paths of your feet." Let a bishop's splendour be attested by deeds, not by the tongue: the brightness of this office shines more by the evidence of truth than by that of speech. You see, then, how safe is the position of one who is under authority, and with how many perils that of the one set over others is bound up. You will be able to support my duties more with your sighs than with your applause. Let no one think that what panders to the ears is excellent: our speech, unless it heals the soul, is worthless. Prefer the one who, with a spiritual sickle, clears the inner self of brambles. His diadem is precious when the church's flock, as it advances toward virtue, does not resist his persuasion. The one who follows his teachings loves his admonisher [?] without pretence and with no need of words. Add to this that my inexperience rightly fears the very newness of the office. Only lately brought from the sheepfolds to be readied to guard them, I am learning to be anxious over the needs of all, and I, who could scarcely be relied on to look after myself, am taking up the office of one who must fear for everything. We know how much humbler toward those who serve must be the one who is called to religious command. Whoever has the duty of commanding in this way must yield even to persons of the lowest condition. For the teacher of the Gentiles says: "I have become all things to all, that I might win all." Only may the working of God be present to its own gift, and make worthy the one whom it did not find worthy of so high an office.
PRAYER FOR THE MASS

It is right and just. It is truly right that, at the beginning of our office, we should make supplication to you, Lord of beginnings. You began the infancy of the world itself, as it came forth into new light, from the secret store of your goodness, and you established it with power equal to that secret. The tender beginning of the world stood in wonder at itself and almost tottered, shaken by amazement at its own beauty. Before it knew its order, it had received from its Author only its substance. It asked under what governance the light given to it was to revolve, what end of day time would receive, whether it would be forever reborn through endless settings, and whether night, wrapping the world in its dusky embraces, would not hold it perpetually as its original possession. In this uncertainty, so that things long confused might serve fixed times, the will of our God became law: every ordering, fixed within appointed bounds, could do just as much as he who created it allowed. So, loving Maker, at the outset of our priestly title shine on us with the sun of right living. From our merits let the day of our office gleam in a cloudless sky. By no stealthy assault, by no flatteries of the devil, let what we are called be lost. Let it not be possible for us to commit what is unbecoming. At your command let zeal for what is right pass into nature. Let our deeds be equal to our duties. With our service well ordered, let our blessed authority grow, and let the one who stands foremost in dignity not fall below it in his conduct. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.
PRAYER BEFORE MASS

God, giver of good things, for whom to will is already to accomplish, you consecrated Moses from the midst of the people in the role of prophet. For while he complained of his weakness, he grew strong through your doing. He gained the merit of a high priest while, as witness [?] and judge of himself, he cried out that he deserved nothing, and his humility won for him a summit exalted by his deeds. Grant equal grace to our beginnings, for we declare that our actions deserve a heavier punishment. What we ask is not unheard of; your kindness is bound by the testimony of example. You will be all the more merciful toward us in bestowing good things, the more our nature has been made prone to fall under the burden of sin. Grant, good commander, a strength worthy of your choice, for under a kindly prince no lowliness disgraces a soldier. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.
VI. ADDRESS [ON THE HERETICS AND THE SYNOD]

The silence we kept for good reason must for good reason be broken. To make it clear that both the services of our tongue and our silence have kept their appointed times, we break out into the duty of speech at the urging of faith. For to speak needlessly is the same as not to have spoken when it was needed, as the apostle says: "Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel," and elsewhere: "A time to keep silent" [?]. It befits us especially, whom the weight of a service that sets us above others urges on, either to raise up those who do good or to restrain the wicked. Indeed, to teach you is nothing other than to spur on those who are already running. What you do of your own accord, we would be proud to believe was owed to our instructions. Yet whoever approves good efforts increases them. You know well in your consciences how gravely Nestorius and Eutyches, twin monsters of the devil's shaping, long corrupted the chaste discipline of the Eastern churches with the fornication of faithlessness. As the apostle says, they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, and therefore God sent them the working of error, so that they believed a lie. Meanwhile that field of contention tests the soldiers of Christ through the stealthy occasion of scandal, as it is written: "There must be contests, so that those who are approved may be made manifest." In whom does the venerable memory of the Council of Chalcedon not live? At that council Dioscorus and his followers were condemned by the pen of holy strictness, and the city of Constantinople joyfully received the venerable remains of Flavian of holy memory, whose verdict heavenly decrees had long since confirmed. Where in the world is Timothy unknown, who did not shrink from becoming worse than a parricide by murdering Proterius of revered memory? By persecuting a holy bishop he surpassed every kind of crime and every name for it. Known too are Peter and Cyrus and Timothy, who, in stretching out a hand to the fallen Dioscorus, fell with him: from their predecessor they inherited both his pursuits and his ruin. Therefore, brothers, hold fast to the judgement of the fathers, which abides in heaven and clings to blessed Peter, for we desire the unity of a pure church that has no stain. We cannot patiently bear those who belch out vain and blasphemous things against our Christ. We know that whoever does not use the remedy of the knife on rotting limbs does service to creeping disease: unless putrefied parts are cut away, they infect the rest. Combat with those who strive to attack what is right is a peaceful kind of combat. Who would be held back by the barrier of fear from such wars, in which he may rejoice in a life-giving death? To what powers of this world should we think we must yield, even if they threaten, when he who governs kingdoms commands otherwise? As the apostle says: "The sufferings of this world are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in us." The things of this present life either trouble or delight the unstable hearts of churchmen. Among them is Acacius, who, moved from his position by the dreadful command of the devil, came to be ashamed that he had long been a champion of truth. Abandoning the honours of a glorious struggle, he defeated his own triumph, which he had earned by pious toil under Basiliscus. Almost at the very moment of attaining his rewards he begrudged them to himself, cutting down the hope of good fruit with the sickle of faithlessness. For it is a graver thing to trample on good things once tasted than on those never touched: no defence is left to a man who, after the sweet taste of righteousness, returns to the deadly poisons of schism. From the things we have spoken of arose what is reported to have been committed recently in the church of Constantinople. For this reason we grieve without using our voice: those who do not obey when remedies are offered rightly have no consolation in the time of their distress.
VII. ADDRESS AT THE DEDICATION OF A LECTURE HALL, WHEN IT WAS MOVED TO THE FORUM

As the battlefield trains the soldier, the sea the sailor, and the courts the advocate, and as uncertain chances tempt the robber, so lecture halls exercise the tongue. For what reason, confound it, could counsel silence in a place where prizes are set for words? Where is the palm of oratory, if here silence wins favour? Fittingly are the wages of sweat paid where there are temples of victory; fittingly is servitude driven out among the halls of liberty. Here only a captive mind would keep its mouth bound: whoever still falls silent as though in some retreat does not know the forum of the Roman people or the school of liberal learning. Inns, perhaps, may be mute; here nothing is so familiar as the pageantry of speech. The applause that is the spirit of the customary performance urges people to bring Fescennine jests to wedding songs. Warriors are roused by bugles; the deep song of trumpets lifts up those who are weak in courage. Every undertaking has been given its fitting incentives. What am I to do, best of teachers, when you are speaking? If I keep my unpolished words shut up in a modest inner chamber, you would not recognize me as one formed by your teaching. If I am sparing with my thanks, I shall offend the sacred bond of friendship by paying neither the honours due to the festival of this move nor the tribute of praise owed to you. Hail, then, nurturer of progress, torch and splendour of noble breeding! You clear noble shoots with toiling hoes and make them known by their fruits. In the white blossom of a young generation you show how much is being prepared for the granaries. You call us back to the forum from the lairs of wild beasts and the haunts of owls, the forum that our ancestors had left long ages ago. For these halls do not lie open to scholars on whom they themselves have bestowed learning only at the lip's edge [?]. Whose trumpet of eloquence would be recognized unless the boyish rudiments of his speech had first become known? To you, then, we owe these benefits: that the advocate, when he is about to summon a defendant, will begin his speech as a man to be feared, in halls where he has already been proved. To you must be credited the one hope of an honourable profession: that the nobility, after a brief course of time, will win approval through the sweat of liberal study. But where is my affection for you sweeping me, ignorant of my own strength and heedless of the ocean of the subject? It is enough to have declared my good wishes at the celebration of a friendly place and day. I turn back to you, students, to whom, moved by fatherly affection, I owe a voice of admonition. By study make yourselves worthy of your origin; by reading make yourselves worthy of your birth. Let the radiance of eloquence display the light of your nature. Multiply your parents' honours by advancing in knowledge; adorn the glories of your ancestors with learning. Unless the craftsman's hand brings it to perfection, the nobility of golden metal is almost dulled by the darkness of its mother earth, and if it is not made beautiful by a master's polish, the excellence granted by its vein profits it nothing. A teacher's diligence is indeed helped by the gifts of purer blood, but unless they are filed smooth, the qualities raised up by the privilege of birth do not glow. A peasant child drains its mother's breasts among the furrows and, while still hanging at the breast, grows used to driving cattle through the pastures. It is carried in its father's arms while he wearies the bullocks; it grasps the right hand that commits great seeds to the earth, and on the very threshold of life it practises the sweat of its forebears. What, then, should you do, whom excellent mothers bore for liberal studies? You will be strangers to your richer stock unless your training shows you to be noble. You have a teacher to lead you in eloquence and in morals. Run, spurred on by your lineage, and when the promised prizes have brought you to the contest, deign to remember me, for there is support that your encourager may receive from you after the heavenly reward. These are the things about which I have been permitted to admonish you in my words. Weigh the care of my heart by considering my words. Do not be delighted by ornate speech, or by a narrative that is merely seductive and painted with cosmetics. Seek from me not what is pleasant but what is necessary, not what is dainty but what is strong. Does pageantry help a man who is about to give precepts? Whoever arranges to be approved no more for his thoughts than for his style empties the role of an admonisher of its meaning. Let the speech of one who corrects be adorned with weight; let whoever longs to be heard hold the scales when he exhorts. Let the teacher of virtue shut out applause: a speech of good character commands what it urges. If I cannot set these things out by skill in speaking, I have nonetheless learned to love them by reflecting on their aim and by choosing their counsel. It is a part of virtue to know what is better, even if you cannot carry it out. The accomplishment of the work follows a well-tested intention, and whoever loves the ornaments of learning stands next to the master. But may God join himself as a companion to my prayer, so that what I, as teacher, entrust to these young plots I may pluck as fruit, as if from an inherited estate.
VIII. PREFACE SPOKEN FOR LUPICINUS WHEN HE WAS HANDED OVER IN THE LECTURE HALL TO THE DISTINGUISHED DEUTERIUS

Whenever the little flower of amomum or a crop of cassia is robbed of its root by a wanton thumb's plundering, and the noble shoot is added to the dowry of human hands, it shows the merit of its soil by its scent and proves the genius of its nature at first sight. A lofty offspring does not suffer itself to be hidden; the beauty of illustrious blood is not kept concealed; the voice of a pure origin is always heard, even in hidden places. Yet although this is so, it belongs to human kindness not to keep silent about what delights you. He takes on little burden who commends what he knows to be worthy of love; he does not escape the stain of savagery who does not hasten to affirm what he knows will please by its merits. Who would refuse to praise the day? Who would fear to extol the sun's rays in any night of speech? If speech pays homage to its theme, it takes its dignity from the theme. So do not be troubled by the leanness of your own talent, since the cheapness of your eloquence is raised by the worth of the subject you have taken up. Rise, my mind, weighed down by the burden of inexperience; my right hand, you are relieved of the load laid upon you. But why do we wrap ourselves in long words? The foregoing account serves the present youth, who, I promise myself, will return to the standard of his forefathers—not by the pronouncement of augurs, but, after God, sustained by hope in your perfection. Nor do I doubt that you can restore to him the splendor of his own people that you have conferred on others; for one who is able to build new glories can easily revive those of the ancients. Do not think these are merely the provocations of eloquence. To you alone it has been granted either to give or to restore the distinction of ancestors. Before your eyes stand not the boy's ancient monuments but recent ones. Firminus and Licerius, the stars of their age, address your skill with these words:

"Receive, most learned of men, the shoot of both families, and attend favorably to the stalk on which you may bring forth heavy ears of grain. Scratch the rich soil with hoes; if it is the fiber [?] of our stock, it will surely bear a crop that answers your labors. Teach the wedded seedlings to grow under the moist bark; fit the fruit of a better scion into the teeth of the young sapling; let a yield of fruit follow, while under your teaching the loftier plant is bitten by the tender mouth of the cleft. For unless the farmers' mattocks have written upon the tamed earth three and four times, thorn and darnel will overcome the wheat harvest. Cultivation enriches the gift of Pallas and the hoary groves with abundant berries. India nourishes with much sweat the ebony it boasts of. The Sabaeans' twig of incense does not thrive when the hand is idle. Industry has made the thornbrakes bear roses for the people of Paestum, which labor draws out of thorns like stars of the earth. Happy is the persistence of the worker whenever his hand is laid to rich clods. Then his tired arms swell with the sap of overflowing health, when the fields pay the farmers their interest in full. [?] the desire for the earth's fertility [?]: the ploughshares must be driven so that autumn's dowry may abound along the vine-shoots. No one ever earned must foaming at the lip except the one who cut back the vines' luxuriance with the curved pruning-hook and, in his various labors, poured out more liquid in sweat than he received in wine. Such is the nature of mortals. The first beginnings of little children are rightly compared to young trees: once the care of parents has plucked them from the mother's root, they must consider to what soil they will entrust them according to their wishes. After deliberation we transfer our rights to teachers. Then those whom nature has granted to us become yours by instruction; then the file of studies begins to claim for itself as much as birth can scarcely achieve. Indeed it is hardly unjust that lineage should be outdone when compared with learning, since the father's office has indulgence for its companion, the teacher's has diligent care: the parent is made for delights, the instructor for labors; birth bestows freedom, the counselor makes one worthy of freedom. What is praised in a man, therefore, is more yours: for if the testimony of eloquence is lacking, no one will be able to proclaim his birth. The tongue you bestow displays a family's splendor; the master's kindness becomes the herald of a lineage; unlearned nobility forswears a heavenly gift. So bind with tighter bonds the straying of a shoot that wanders with the years; prune with iron the branches that bear no offspring; raise the young turf with the warmth by which you make all things fruitful. Our youth, whichever of his kin he looks to, has people to follow. Believe us, driven by so many spurs he will fly across whatever sea of knowledge he enters; he will be goaded by the spurs of his lineage; through so many ranks of ancestors he will find nothing that does not invite him to letters. Behold, our little one stands before you, to be initiated under happy auspices, and like the victim of a righteous man he calls for a priest's devotion. With his face he appeals to fatherly affection, that it may by some speech commend his childhood, set on the threshold of life. He asks this of his elders not in words, but his trembling shows what he wants: we are compelled to come to the aid of the little one in the need that his fear reveals. Young man, pledge to your people things worthy of your beginnings: we conceive solid hope of your perfection; we hand over a good talent to the best of teachers. Now revere the first rudiments of this sacred company: those whom you see showing their future light with modest sparks advance to become stars of the Latin senate. Let it suffice to have said this to you all; for me there remains a brief recommendation. I have presented to you one who is my kin as his kinsman, one bereft of his parents as a man of religion. You already know what makes me feel affection for the boy. If kinship is considered, I cannot be free of love; if piety is the friend of my calling, those stripped of their parents' protection become our sons. So one bond comes from lineage; by another, duty binds us. Look, venerable master, at so many hands raised in supplication for him, and in the hope placed in this little one consider his elders, myself and you. The learning of a pupil is a singular kind of praise for teachers. Chiron became known through the tongue of Achilles: the merit of the follower made the repute of the master more beloved, whose eloquence perhaps could not have come to light by itself. Your Maro commended his teachers as greatly as he himself is known, and certainly fame would not have made them known by their own merits. Our Jerome, had he not called Gregory his teacher, would be judged better than he; but the good qualities of the one named must be credited to him from whom they seem to have taken their origin. In sum, as I said, a master's renown strikes the heavens through the perfection of his pupil. Before one who knows these things I do not charge you with forgetfulness, since I recall what is known; those who love are greedy even for what they know. I pray God to join his grace as companion to your studies, so that you may make most learned those you have received from me to be polished, and that their learning may become your glory indeed, but my service."
DICTIO IX: PREFACE DELIVERED WHEN ARATOR ENTERED THE LECTURE HALL

It is well known to all mortals that leisure from business gives birth to the labor of speaking, and that when the storms of cares are banished, the calm skies of oratory shine all the brighter. Talents do not lose their daylight unless they are darkened by the clouds of business: the radiance of thoughts shines on those free from care, and an unencumbered mind lends splendor to the pomp of declamation. He who boldly cleaves the blind straits with his oars applies to the helm a breast free of anxiety and weighs the steering of the tiller with that single attention which befits a ship's master. Then the hempen reins are loosed to the winds as he wishes; then seas long free are bound with the bonds of rigging, and man enters to master the imperious heaps of waves, to learn the uncertain ways as the stars reveal them. Then, watching the Bosporus [?], the Pleiades, Cynosura, and whatever shows the way, man's path is set by the guidance of heaven—provided only that his mind is gnawed by no doubt arising from outside business, and that grief, the teacher of sloth, does not afflict his knowledge on its journey. But if the mind either sleeps, dulled by lazy torpor, or is roused by various goads and dragged off along byways, it cannot meet its purpose wholly, since anxiety, the butcher of souls, tears apart the limbs of its prudence. He is always ineffective, and shows himself cut off from the strength of his own bulk, who cannot display in the form of his compositions how great he is. Yet it is the part of a good teacher to weigh the source of a winding stream that is brought to him by a nail scratching the earth, to judge what its channel is when gathered into one and what it is where it rises, and to reckon the river's strength not from what it has received but from what it could have received. If you ask, venerable master, guarantor of liberty, witness of good blood, file of talents, fashioner of minds, why I have set out these words: I have spoken of myself, myself, I confess; I have described myself, whom, in the infancy of a slumbering ignorance, various occupations and sorrow, the strong mother of unskill, have weighed down—a man who is not allowed to free his neck from harsh labors so that his mouth may be graced with the bit of studies. That my speech is rough and gleams with no polish of diction is due to understanding and practice that I am unlearning. You, in your own palaestra, are spurred on by the palm of eloquence that is yours by birth; you proud Delos counts among her citizens, forgetful of me. You walk abroad as the sumptuous owner of the Castalian flood, while I, with lips all but parched, let fall a trickling drop of stale liquid. The harvest of learning enriches you, as its own farmer, through constant sweat with no distraction intervening; but to me a pauper's meal of beans is barely handed out from the granaries of the great. You have been appointed as a fortunate right hand to support a liberty about to fall; a corner of the church encloses me, who fear even the good things of this present age. Why, I ask, did you see fit some while ago to turn the distinguished eyes of your eloquence on me, placed so far away? There were others, rather, whom the ornaments of your diction might shape, to whom the trappings of words acquired through Latin elegance would give a name destined to live on even among posterity. It befits me only to be held by silent affection, unequal to speaking and set apart from public duties. Why rouse a spirit that another order of life had already made subject to itself? Why call back across long stretches of road a distant man, for whom, just as it is a sin not to have deserved praise, so it is a crime to have been praised? These things belong to you, to you, do not doubt it—or to those who follow you, if any such could be found. Yet, if you will pardon me, I turn my words to the youth whom the auspices of this present day have dedicated to your lecture hall, with whom I share a like infancy of speech. Though I commend his beginnings in unwrought speech, I am excused by the commands of love. We are sent under the yoke, constrained by the necessity of affection, and while we look out for those dear to us, we do not see what becomes us. Although a father's speech ought to have accompanied him, the one I offer is not foreign to a father. My calling too, my fine boy, owed you a speech. Happy is that omen of a name among the learned: destined to be enriched with the fruits of knowledge, he promises by his very name the labor that studies require. Cleave, excellent young man, the backs of rich lands; drive in the tooth of the ploughshare, formed on an anvil still new; practice in the soil of studies whatever befits the best of ploughmen. If you search deeply into the secrets of hidden fields, you will find there Deuterius, who by the richness of his eloquence will repay you with seeds multiplied and reward the sweat you have spent. Learn now to cut back the luxuriance of words with the pruning-hook of art, so that the young turf may thrive under the discipline of iron. Let whatever the barren shade of shoots has put forth be cut away; let your vines stretch out their branches only for the hope of grapes. Such you must return to your nature; such you must answer our hopes, and when you have adorned yourself with heavy ears of knowledge, then it will be fitting that you be called a great Arator, a great ploughman. Therefore let the hope of reward nourish in you an ardor for praise. Read [?], because it is no sport of fortune if ever a lettered man rises among the dreg-laden herds of the unskilled, of whom I am the first. Do not fear the oppression by which the educated are weighed down: learning laid low has more praise than the high places of rustics. Their own conscience lifts up the learned, and if ever they are set against the uncertain blasts of the times, they endure evils that are to be charged to the age rather than to their deserts.

Some say that the address I composed—a truly rustic one—in commending Arator was mere flattery of a fortunate person, whose favor a necessity masquerading as affection sought to win because of his father's power; that in this service of praise, serving only the living and present, my tongue displayed a servility of the moment—a tongue that, whenever it plays with painted images of words in praising someone, conceals with all the greater zeal what the mind has conceived. For sometimes the pen gives the learned a deeper hiding place for their thoughts, when it beguiles the ears of the undeserving with sweet poultices. But let such practices be kept far from our purpose. We ought both to know them and to hate them, for the prudent avoid what is known more carefully than what is unforeseen. As for me, unless love supplies me with words for praising friends—words dictated in the inner recesses of conscience with charity as teacher—I shall stumble along the paths of my compositions beneath the burden of the task I have undertaken. Therefore to my noble friend, whom my own talent has served without deceit, I brought speeches that reveal my mind, since friendship between equals is free from suspicion of flattery, and the faithful sincerity of those who love is proven whenever what one might fear does not come from power. With me, a man of rank earns nothing by command that he does not lay on me by kindness. Some, however, say that a man of religion ought rather to have offered his words to the faithful orphan when he began, under good auspices, the schools of letters. I called him bereft of his parents—he for whom, through nature's happy losses, the common father and bishop has become his own. That consolation of the afflicted, food of the hungry, eye of the blind, foot of the lame, has turned all the forms of his piety and all the degrees of his mercies to this boy's advancement. And that genius of the lord Laurentius which relieves the needs of the world is exercised in the service of this little child. To whom, I can truly say, would such a calamity not be welcome? Whom would it not please to have lost a father, if by a profitable exchange he is granted to find such a one? The distinctions of so great a man, which I cannot do justice to, I will not profane with unworthy words. He it is whose authority is sweet or whose sweetness is stern; who fills the part of master in church, master at home, master at table, master in jest; who never does what he would not wish his followers to imitate; whose conduct, polished to perfection, shows his disciples the road to heaven as he walks it—for it is lesser praise to teach well unless you show by deeds what is to be taught. Taken up by this man, what would my speech have added to the youth, for whom a favorable outcome awaits from the merits of his teacher, and perfection from the good fortune of his orphanhood? For him his patron's prayers are enough, through which, steeped in the best teaching, he will deserve to rise loftily above his birth.
DICTIO X: THANKSGIVING TO THE GRAMMARIAN WHEN PARTHENIUS RECITED WELL

When we render the thanks due for benefits received, I believe that in serving our kin we renounce boasting; for no swelling of arrogance is cloaked in the garment of honor when words serve not glory but blood. It is one thing to speak so as to be praised, another to speak so as not to be blamed. In the first case, a mind greedy for fame is in thrall to boasting; in the second, with reason preserved, it rightly turns into a matter of glory whatever has come from the sweat of speaking. For favor is shown to just and to superfluous declamations alike, even if in equal words, yet with discerning minds: the praises of a tyrant and of good princes are celebrated by one and the same mouth, and there is no difference between the encomia of him who deserves them and of him who usurps them. Unless the weighty judgment of those who assess them weighed the causes of speaking, this breeze of applause, which falls even to the unworthy, would make no distinction. The hidden purposes of speeches are examined by hearers not with the tongue but with the heart. In short, it is one thing to listen to a speaker pleasantly and gladly, another to approve the feeling with which he speaks. But now, setting aside commendations of my theme, let the infancy of my mediocrity speak rather of the matter itself. Some time ago, excellent master, I brought Parthenius to you, eager for your studies, with the recommendation of my little speech, at the time when he was crossing the threshold of the liberal disciplines, when it was still uncertain whether he would declare the luster of his lineage through learning; for a man whose blood is not revealed by his education has no witness to his nobility. We accompanied him with a speech, then, at a time when it was not possible for our words to show what kind of birth he had, since it is always a blot on good merits to have the light of noble blood yet be shut in the night of rusticity, to be proclaimed by the voices of pedigrees yet lie hidden in the darkness of ignorance. Gold is nothing unless it is shaped by the craftsman's hand, and value is joined to the tawny metal by the working of the file: when industry ceases, the brilliance that comes from nature is slight. The earth owes to the smith's craft the praise it wins for what it brings forth: by the benefit of the furnace, what passes from the hidden brood of the veins into the form of solid iron is tamed, and it in turn takes captive the wild hearts of men with a taming affection. [?] they would not provide sustenance to mortals unless their backs were worked. It is the work of art that man enters the liquid element of the sea without fear and, through ingenuity, overcomes the road of death with little danger. The simple skill of farmers, while marking out the face of the earth with their arms, lays out vineyards and wrings from the offspring of trees the liquid by which health is nourished. By many signs it is shown that the diligence of workers either pours in what birth did not give or preserves the good things it did give. And if such is the universal condition of things, how highly, most learned teacher, must your care be exalted with praise, by whose right hand liberty, now on the very point of falling, is raised up again; by whose skill new things are established or the glories of ancestors preserved? I truly confess that, were it not for you, whatever displays talent would soon succumb. But why do I bind myself to the greatest matters, I who cannot bear small ones, and offer a general thanksgiving when I am scarcely equal to thanking for one person? Before many witnesses, most correct of men, I give you abundant thanks, because by your teaching you have made me recognize Parthenius. You removed thorns and darnel from his breast with the hoe of knowledge; you raised a wheat harvest with which he may feed his kin, happily showing him, amid the discord of his families, one thing to follow and another to flee. O power of your talent, praiseworthy beyond human measure! In one and the same person, with what art you showed him what to learn and what to unlearn, since both came down to him through his blood! May God bring our joys to a happy outcome; far be whatever adversity threatens. You are to be praised the more because your pupil knows how to avoid his lineage than because he strives to imitate it. Behold, Parthenius's kinship, descending to him by both paths of his ancestry, he happily acknowledges in some things and happily disowns in others. How I feared that this mixture, at odds within its very diversity, would see the better part defeated and yield to the rule of the worse, and that, given the meanness of the times, the untaught part would more easily reign in him! But you, the ornament of your age, have shown me that I obtained more for my kinsman than I asked. You have imitated heaven in the abundance of your kindness, since with manifold outlay you surpassed the wishes of the one who commended him. Behold, now from a wintry breast and a frozen heart the little flowers of eloquence bloom as in spring, and the smiling buds of words paint the baskets that display them; behold, after barbarian muttering, words that betoken humanity pour from his mouth. If I do not make a return for these gifts of yours, you may judge that you bestowed them on one who did not deserve them. For whoever receives greater successes with a tongue that keeps holiday shows that he does not love what good fortune has brought him.
DICTIO XI: DELIVERED WHEN THE SON OF EUSEBIUS WAS HANDED OVER FOR HIS STUDIES

Things long interrupted, like new things, bring their own dread. When a speaker's confidence shrinks back from the friction of public favour, he becomes again what he was before he learned, and as the habit of speaking dies away, old age is led back to the infancy it once struggled out of. A colt trained for the Olympic contests is confident of the palm, and unless idleness weakens it, it believes victory is its by right. Hope always promises it the crown with persuasive enticements, unless the languor of sloth strips the prize from its speed. The skilled javelin-thrower, sure of his triumphs, longs for uncertain contests, and the man whom glory always meets in the battle line is overcome by a long peace. Constant practice, the nurse of talent, adorns the poets' ivy with nobler clusters and a greener look; when practice stops, even a proven advocate falls silent. The sailor raised on ships [crosses?] the liquid sea without fear, but if he turns his life to duties on land, he no longer reads his courses by the stars or the winds by their signs. If a farmer, lured by the refinements of the city, ever comes to despise the plough, he will be dragged off course while he scores the backs of his oxen. So just as persistence is found to be the mother of every art in its own work, neglect is the stepmother of learning. Such is the condition of this speech of mine, which I bring out after a long interval. It brings no familiar figures; it displays none of the pomp it should have bought with age. It places all its trust in the kindness of its hearers and believes that indulgence is enough in place of applause, and devout wishes enough in place of merit. Away with you, feeble fear! Pity for an orphan [?] commends him, and a sacred duty commends the speech. What could even a speech endowed with the splendour of skill achieve here, where the cause pleases without the help of a persuasive tongue? The matter itself has won favour; it is enough that the words earn goodwill, and both have come to your hearing under favourable omens. I will indeed say what remains, since whatever is left unsaid in the present cause I will be taking away from my own praises. His most noble father Eusebius, a father as much in character as by nature, wished, when pressed by his last hours, to overcome the lot of humanity by a plan that would bring benefit long after. While by the vigour of his living soul he was treading down the narrow confines of his earthly prison and, called by God, was pouring himself back into the spiritual dwellings, nothing human remained in his mind except a spotless love for his son, the one thing that no forgetfulness erases even among the heavenly beings. Then, as one who knew me well, he left this boy to me to cherish, as [?]. The words of the man entrusting him were mingled with his last sighs. Let others see to what he left them; to me, under solemn appeal to God, he left his heir. As the boy touches the taste of life with the edge of his lips, I pray that the taste of liberal learning may be poured into him, so that, drawn on by the honey of the disciplines and by the combs of knowledge from their waxen houses, he may take for himself the nectar of that flowing element. Venerable teacher, through him your praise, brought to its height, has something to gain. The fullness of your merits does not refuse increase from the progress of such pupils, since a pupil's polish is the unblemished vindication of his teacher, and above all of this one, whose splendid lineage the time now demands that you adorn with the rays of learning, so that the glory of his origin may advance into a most serene day once the brilliance of eloquence has shone forth in him.
XII. A SPEECH GIVEN TO ARATOR WHEN HE ADVANCED TO THE EXERCISE OF PRAISE. COMPOSED ON THE DAY.
THEME: IN PRAISE OF LETTERS.
PREFACE.

Let shining Letters be praised from their own wealth,
For outside adornment will add nothing to their genius.
Dyed silks shine brighter when a Chinese wears them;
Gleaming gems become a Persian's neck.
It is no gain to deck the limbs with borrowed lustre:
It is their own natural light that makes the stars noble.
NARRATION.

All things judged worthy of public praise should be praised as well as one's power of speech allows. Radiant Letters must be repaid what they are owed out of the dowry of eloquence, for just as a free gift reveals both the wealth and the spirit of the giver, so denying what one has received exposes the greed and shamelessness of the one who withholds it. Let us pour out to the divinity of Letters what has flowed from their own altars. However great the abundance of praise with which this subject is honoured, however richly the words overflow, it is fed and filled from the produce of its own estate. While, among the green places it has laid out, it captivates the eye with its own loveliness, it does indeed take delight in its own grasses, but the harvests of talent receive greater increase through their mistress. So whoever pays interest to Letters grows richer, since the streams directed to them are brought back through hidden passages as through great channels, and what you let out drop by drop you will possess as fully as if you held rights over the ebbing Ionian Sea. Who would refuse to pay out the deposit of learning, unless he wants to become a beggar by hoarding it? The fruit of this thing, wonderful to say, surges into abundance when it is poured out, while it leaves those who brood over it starving. Therefore, venerable art, after heavenly help, after the aid of favour from above, supply the praises you are to enjoy, and rejoice in the good of your own invention, in what you yourself have sent forth. Embrace, in the work of praise, what has sprung from you: nothing remains to us in this matter that deserves either punishment or reward. If by the faithful service of our mouths we offer too little in exalting your merits, that is what you gave us. We are the pipes of these streams, and we drink none of the abundance of the water entrusted to us. So that through us you may do justice to your merits, flow in like the Aegean Sea, like the spring of Pegasus. They are before your eyes, if you rightly keep in mind the examples of your own ways. Whatever jewels from your wealth we put out at interest are safe. See, a diadem gleaming with your light ennobles my head, and with the varied brilliance of its precious stones it grows by its own genius when it is fittingly displayed. From you the teachings of wisdom take their root; through you, once shaped, they are brought forth. Without you the heart has no savour and speech no freedom. You are the testimony of free-born blood, you are the stuff of modesty; through you the tongue speaks out what the heart has rightly dictated. You provide the way to search out justice, clearing the path, choked with thorns, by which heavenly things are sought. You make a crop of wheat out of tares, fertile clods out of barren minds, and carry heavy ears of grain to the granaries of knowledge, so that the famine of speechlessness cannot prevail. By preserving the brightness of a pure family, you flood a base lineage with a light not its own. Something very close to God is poured in by your kindness, since through the course of the learning handed down it is ensured, with the truth of pedigrees kept intact, that the best do not fall away from their kind and that the bad do fall away from theirs. Through you the deeds of the innocent, which served to instruct those who come after, do not perish: by your chains past events are drawn back into public view, and buried things come to life again. You are the instruments of memory, you are the cause of piety; with your ploughshares the soil of the human heart is marked out and prepared for fruitfulness. You are the founders of religion, the enemies of crime. With you as guides, the crimes that steal in through habit are unlearned, you through whom good things are learned. You either drive men toward an upright purpose or change a crooked one. Exiles are honoured by your testimony, and those cut off from the heights of the world you join to heaven. Bad consciences you either disdain to enter, or, having entered, you consecrate them into a sanctuary. Far be it from Letters either to change what is worthy or to leave unchanged what is harmful. No equipment shields those clad in steel from your wounds: you reach the inmost parts even of those whom iron has covered. With your shields the weapons aimed by adversaries are driven back, and no wickerwork of shields can be set against the darts of your skill. You lift up those in affliction; you soothe those placed on the cross of bodily suffering; you so increase joys that cheerfulness, even when prolonged, keeps its due measure. If comforts come from you, they grow sweet. Against your command one may not even weep for a dead loved one. You suit weddings, you suit funerals: the study of this learning holds the most opposite things in harmony, and embracing both, it rejoices. Would that you might be honoured with longer speeches, and that brevity were not owed to your laws, from which comes all the abundance one could wish! Through the shapes of letters a voice meant to travel far is safely entrusted, and it is made firm, with no loss to itself, whenever someone reads it again. Before you, humanity lived ignorant of order, and breasts belching acorns spewed out words without measure. You make a distinction between men of one and the same nature: knowledge of you makes them like the heavenly beings, ignorance of you makes them like cattle. It is plain what the forsaken race of mortals was before this harvest: for those who come into the light on equal terms with us do not, because of the distinction you make, share one and the same condition of wisdom. Farewell, ornaments of a better age; granted by God, possess the world you have cleared of rubble, as a remedy for the times.
XIII. A SPEECH [WHEN PATERIUS AND SEVERUS WERE HANDED OVER TO THEIR STUDIES.]

If a sailor with favouring winds happily crosses the straight course of his voyage over the waters, if greater success leads the warrior to triumph, if the soldier of letters on the fields of rhetoric is raised higher by the judge's favour, then it is ours today to rejoice in equal measure. (On the theme.) What have I to do with the exposed and unworthy poverty of my talent? See, by a happy lot we grow rich from the harvest of the speech we have undertaken, since the merit of the subject magnifies the speaker and the cause commends the pleader. Where is the fear that held us in subjection through awareness of our lack of skill? Where is the trembling of the face, grown weaker through lack of use and practice? We forget our own deserts while we speak of another's renown. Now we learn that the powerful can make others powerful too [?], since noble fame gives so much even to its herald. I have nothing to do with doubts. Splendour lights up those who praise it, and the sun opens up even those sunk in darkness, if they remember it. But once again cheerfulness is joined with fear, and trembling becomes the companion of exultation. When is one unequal to small things sufficient for the greatest? For whoever does not commend renown with the light of his style clouds it over; and just as modest things grow through the talent of the eloquent, so the grandest things lose their charm through dryness, and unless you weigh your strength before taking up a burden, you will sink beneath it. Look: Paterius and Severus, ornaments of the curule chairs, bearers of names inherited from the purple, are awaiting at the very beginning of their lives the education that is theirs by birth, thinking it beneath them not to drink in diligent study along with the first taste of daylight, since nature gave them at one and the same moment to the light of day and to letters. Why should I, as speaker, press upon minds that already know them the honours of their parents and their ancient insignia? I will be relieved of this burden if you, listener, consult the consular records on my behalf. On my side are the centuries; on my side is that solemn acclamation of the Campus; on my side both the palace and the senate-house revere Severus and Paterius. Although their family has earned ivory staffs and consular robes, yet, setting aside for the moment the dowry of their blood, they have won by their character that they know no setting, neither through their offices nor after the grave. I lie, unless Paterius lives on in the esteem of the learned and, cast in lasting bronze, presents among the skilled that likeness ennobled by the palms of eloquence. Their offspring, still small indeed but already very great, showing the jewelled face of a budding little flower, implores the protection of the voice that it will one day provide itself, asking for it by the plea of a silent conversation: "Help the little ones, whom you will soon have as fathers of the fatherland. Spend your protection on your defenders and fight for the tender, lest, when we are riper in years, we fall while fighting for the whole community. You know which house labours hard against the common calamity, to whom thanks are due for the common security, from whom it has flowed that, amid adversity, civil order among you does not waver. Our lineage owes you this tribute, to raise without ceasing guardians for its fatherland. So if the good qualities of our stock are known to you, supply what must be grafted onto it, so that cultivation may improve what shines in the seed and the turf, cooperating with the root, may bear fruit. What it would yield is not foreign; what we ask for is not fleeting. If a colt valued for its sires is reared for the contests of Elis and Olympia, let us be strengthened by the examples of our fathers, who are still advancing. Prosperity has favoured you so greatly that the posterity of your champions is growing up while the protection of father and grandfather has not yet failed." Therefore, venerable teacher, receive the one spurred by these goads, who brings the voices of all, and lend a kindly mind to the pleas of the native soil. Look at our judgments of you, and, lifted up by the thought of your merit, shape yourself to match the opinion of many. Labour so that, under your training, our defences may be made firm, and, so that the hostile assault of battering rams may not prevail, join the arms of study to the walls of the fatherland. We know whose offspring is being entrusted to you; see to it that diligence strengthens what nature has brought forth strong. If one born of a brave man's stock feels fear in war, it will be the fault of his commander, not of his birth. It is enough for you to grow through the sweat of your teaching in such a way that you make [?] these boys before you attain the stature of the ancients. But perhaps you will say: "Although a holier profession presses upon you..." Even so, my concern for these boys does not come last with me. I am the one to whom the womb of the sacred font, at once mother and virgin, brought forth Paterius as a son; I am his father in the second birth, or re-creation, of his soul. Therefore the care of his education concerns me in a special way, since I have been called his father even in heavenly things.
XIV. A SPEECH AGAINST AN ENVOY WHO BETRAYED HIS COUNTRY TO THE ENEMY.

If a crime is graver when committed by a person worthy of reverence, then you have, judges, in one man two utterly opposite things: the deserts of a traitor and the sacred office of an envoy. But my voice is overcome and defeated at the very outset: I can scarcely believe the crime I am charging. Who would think that complete treachery had found its home in a title of integrity? We are forced to say it, since a traitor fears no wrong and a true envoy commits none. Why do you set your title against my accusation as proof of innocence? You could have escaped your pursuer if in your deeds you were what you are called. No one is more safely wicked than the man who hides under the name of loyalty; wrongdoing is practised in safety when it is covered with the cloak of honesty. Away with a purpose that rests on tricks rather than on the mind! Feeble is the defence that leans on the testimony of a bare office, which will avail nothing. It was our own counsels that opened the way for you to become more harmful to your country; we ourselves, while looking for a champion, brought it about that you appeared as a stronger enemy. We would not feel the weight of hostility you have brought on the fatherland, had it not taken its beginning from the sacred bond of friendship.
