We engage foreign adversaries without difficulty; but the man who bursts forth from the fruit of favour into the passion of an enemy finds an unarmed breast. In the very time of the treaty we ourselves brought it about that the common enemy should not be unaware of what burdened our country. For this man, most illustrious judges, would have deserved capital punishment if he had merely performed his assigned office carelessly and, out of weariness, pursued the interests of his fellow citizens half-heartedly. What, then, is it to have revealed to the enemy the inner affairs of the fatherland, when even to have fought for them sluggishly would have been sacrilege? By what torturers must such things be atoned for, when you have destroyed what it is a crime not to have helped? With what varieties of disguise and deadly polish must he be thought to have reached the point where he was believed to fill the role of an envoy? Virtue that is not inborn is usually formed by care and nurture, and what you have done passes into your disposition. So it is with the practice of falsehood: the man who long feigns goodness gains strength from the habit of honesty. You would still have kept up your deceitful goodwill, had you not seen the path to doing harm unlocked by the key of the embassy. It is as if a physician came to bring health to the sick as they lie tossing in fever, and, under the guise of medicine, searched out the life in their inmost parts in order to shut it out. Who, I ask, would not lay open to him the secrets of the vital organs and tell him in what places strength still remains? The man from whom health is sought is handed an easy chance to destroy. Just so, most impure of men, did we arm you against ourselves by opening our inmost secrets. Now, judges, it hangs on your judgment whether one who has surpassed everyone in his sins ought not to surpass all defendants in his punishments. Cut off the crimes that would be born hereafter: from the torment of one will come the correction of all. It is a kind of piety to be stern toward an enemy of the fatherland, lest by sparing him [?] you provoke vices to grow.
XV. A SPEECH AGAINST A STEPMOTHER WHO, WHEN SHE COULD NOT PERSUADE HER HUSBAND TO HATE HIS SON, GAVE POISON TO BOTH.

Here, judges, is the stepmother who, to satisfy her hatreds, does not spare her affections; who, so that her stepson should not escape, chose to involve in his fate the man she loved; who, like the most savage beasts, made mingled deaths her token [?], judging all who could be slaughtered along with her enemy worthy of the lot of death. With its barriers broken, her fury found its exercise, destroying whatever came in its way as though it were marked out for death. Longing to be deadly to everyone, her rage was still growing, had the poisons not run out. The poisons she had found were drunk by two people; nothing remained to be kept for the destruction of others. Ah, how she groaned at the empty cup when she saw so few corpses, angry with herself for having given the dead more of the deadly liquid than was needed to kill them! She sought to draw back from the bowels of the dead, had it been possible, the price of other people's deaths, so that she could spread death among many drop by drop, and so that the noble venom might take possession of the inmost parts of souls. Before she had tried it, the deadly fluid was poured lavishly into the cup; it made her realise what she had wasted when, with an abundance of juices, she had killed only a few. Where on earth was the spirit of conjugal devotion? Where the sacred bond of marriage? The thought of the stepson weighed more with her than the memory of her marriage bed. While she served her savagery, her love for the husband before her was driven out; she believed that something of her stepson could live on in anyone still alive. In her impiety she wanted to throw the light into confusion and, as the world collapsed, to cut down the harvest of the human race, hurling into ruin whatever could go to its setting, wickedly longing to subject our daylight to the ancient laws of Erebus, so that the hated youth might not look upon it even after the underworld. By what steps and what progress in crime did she come down to poison? For a long time she put off his death, which she finally forced on him, as he lay in torment, in place of a kindness. Before that she had afflicted the body of her enemy with whips, hunger and cold; the carrying out of murder was the last stage of a stepmother's indignation. I would wish, judges, to dwell longer on the accusation, were it not that a longer speech would delay the wicked woman's punishment. We do not want her, who must be condemned, to win a truce in the light of life from the time you allow the one pleading. How often, most wicked of women, did you caress your stepson with deceitful embraces, feigning to be his mother? How often did you give him harmless drinks, so that he would take death from your hand without suspicion? You seized the moment of thirst and the need to drink; perhaps he begged you, so that you might hand him death all the sooner; and by granting your stepson's wishes you gained a reputation for compassion. How often did you take the place of a mother so that you could act the stepmother more safely? Guardians of liberty, in a marriage partnership the offspring of one partner is usually cared for as a shared pledge, since the affection the father has won passes over to the son. When wives die, husbands, in their foresight, look for partners in their cares to bring up their posterity, and so they find stepmothers. Yet often under this name a mother comes in who is all the more careful toward another's offspring the more anxiously she wishes to avoid that tragic name. A natural mother is protected by security and by the sacred bond of her name. There are some who are believed to be angry even out of compassion. Ill-omened women, we rightly spurn your endearments, with which you clothe your inner selves in the paint of malice. I blush, most holy judges, to keep up a long attack on one already condemned by her own deeds; the verdict I am delaying with my efforts is not in doubt. Would that she might be driven from the light by exquisite tortures, and, cut by slow wounds, outlive her own body! Let her guilty soul not be driven from its dwelling all at once. Purity is restored to men's hearts whenever you cleanse the eyes of the public by the punishment of the guilty.
XVI. A SPEECH AGAINST A MAN WHO DEMANDED MARRIAGE TO A VESTAL VIRGIN AS HIS REWARD.

Do you believe, judges, that through this man laments are being mingled with our victories, and that the taste of triumph is soured by the reward? Do you suppose that the gods are offended by how things turned out, and that the divine powers who answered our prayers are being driven to repentance? Here stands the most worthless of men. He commands us to groan because he conquered the enemies of our fatherland. Now that the battles are over, while he demands the price of his labour, he makes us look kindly on enemies and wars alike. He thinks the rewards of labour worthless unless they are granted in defiance of the angry gods, so that his city may lose what it is believed to have gained through him. He is sure that a warrior's spirit is not captured by painted panels and portraits, and he does not ask to be preserved for the ages cast in bronze. The only joys he recognises are those that yield the reward of adultery. If you threw yourself into danger for this purpose, so that what you demand for your sweat is shameful even to name, then we cannot owe our victory to harlots. You did not wage war out of devoted love, you who, after the enemy, now do shameful battle in the middle of the city. In vain did you drive off the enemy, since you play their part in your triumph. We kept our honour free while we were exposed to danger. If this is the good fortune of brave men, it must be shunned, for through it we are joined to the miseries of the conquered. Indeed, lights of the senate, do we suppose that this man was led by small steps of crime to such monstrous desires? By how many stages did practised wickedness arrive at this, that he would buy vices with his feats of glory? We believed, while he spent his life in tents and drove his body through hard successes toward the badges of valour, that he was bound by love of his fellow citizens, so that through his soldiering neither would fire take hold of our cities nor defilement of the sacred virgins. For with all those wounds he bought only this: that no one else should reap the harvest of these crimes. What I owe you, cruellest of men, is plain to see: thanks to your services I, the victor, lament the fate of the vanquished. Tell me, champions of liberty, what terror above all gripped our minds amid the blare of trumpets, while the harvest of iron and the snorting of horses threatened destruction? I believe it was this: that the hard grip of chains should not bind the free necks of our fathers; that the inviolable modesty of our mothers should not perish in the sack of the city; that virginity vowed and consecrated to sacred rites should not be seized by a plunderer's fire; that chastity in service should not become the prize of an insulting enemy; that hostile violence should not carry off bodies freed from the human condition, and that chastity, dragged to the last extremity, should not serve an enemy's lust. I ask you, great-souled hero: what evil did you drive from your fatherland, if as victor you desired the very things I feared, while the favour of the gods assigned the enemies' deaths to your blows? I ask whether in that crisis you begged the gods above to support you. If you did, now that the dangers are past, do you threaten their priests instead of making the offering you owe? If you brought no pious vows to the battle, what do I owe you, whom the common good fortune, by its companionship, delivered without your prayers? If you understand it, you owe much to the gods if they favoured a suppliant, and more if they gave victory to one who did not ask. I suppose that when you came away from battle you first went and worshipped at the shrines and gave thanks there, the very place from which you now strive to snatch plunder with hands that should be at rest. I fear that, though no temple has been burned by any torch, good fortune itself will lead a Vestal virgin away as a captive.
XVII. A declamation against a man who withheld food from his aged father. Given to Arator.

I do not know, judges, whether any penalty can be found that would answer to the crimes of the accused. Meanwhile my tongue lacks words, since the novelty of the deed outstrips the accuser. This is the son who refused sustenance to his aged father though he could have provided it, adding this kind of wickedness to his crimes: that he should be a parricide while his father still lives. You think that because you did not bring death on your parent you have escaped the punishment you deserve. You spared him only to be more guilty. You could have ended the torments you inflicted with your father's final end, had you dealt the death-blow with a healing hand. But this is the first of your evil inventions: neither to ward off your own father's death, as a dutiful son should, nor to inflict it, as a cruel one would. Why is it, inventor of refined danger, that between the two paths you follow neither, and feed upon your father's drawn-out wasting away? Thanks to your management your father lived all the more unhappily, because thanks to your management he was not granted death. No one, most holy judges, doubts that the evils of this world are buried when death is called upon, and that our common lot is what those placed in adversity pray for: what puts an end to bitterness must needs be desired. I ask, then: to what beasts is he to be compared who by his management inflicts hardship without end? Whose schemes, while his hand refrains from the author of his life, have produced a life that one would gladly exchange for death? This man's father was already crushed by the burden of years. Already the ravages of age had brought down, through the old man's trembling limbs, a step once robust. Already, under the long gnawing of time, the face that once declared the man was sinking into wrinkles. Yet he had not reached old age without hope of support, for a grown son was now smiling upon him. Relying on a surer trust, he gave away what he had gathered for his living, for we know that he always placed his granaries in the eagerness of his child. He thought it an ill omen to worry about his property while his son was alive and well. He believed that this would be enough for his cold white hairs: renewed in his offspring's greener years, he no longer had to earn anything himself. Then suddenly this fine young man stripped his father of that security. I should like, venerable judges, to turn my words to him for a moment, but I think warnings offered to ruined morals are wasted. Do we suppose, most venerable of men, that anyone's offspring is brought to these duties by teaching? Nature's instruction is enough for offspring, since human law pours into their hearts what teachers usually impart. For him, fulfilling what is owed is no chance good, nor can what we see implanted in birds be lacking in those endowed with reason. We read that eagles, in turn, are fed by the service of their young, and that the kindnesses of their parents, which the featherless chicks received when they shed the shells of their eggs, they repay with a kind of strict justice. Birds do not think themselves free to refuse what they have received: what sort of nature is it that cannot imitate the winged creatures in caring for its own? I pass over the many examples of the greed of wolves: with fasting mouths they carry food to their parents, and the beast, its own belly unfed, runs to its begetters with a laden mouth. Consider for yourselves the nature of the case and what penalty befits one who has committed unheard-of deeds. For vices spread through impunity, and unless the judge's censure came to the rescue, the force of sin would run through the whole body of society.
XVIII. A declamation against a tyrant who, by way of reward, gave a parricide a statue among the brave men. Given to the most distinguished Arator.

Judges, the likenesses of brave men are preserved in bronze that will last forever, and through these images even the buried know no death. By these arts the image of mortals passes into eternity, and skill overcomes the narrow law of human nature. And yet when has a parricide ever earned the prize of valour, or a tyrant ever paid it? When has the reward of the innocent been wrung out by a criminal or forced on him by an oppressor of liberty? A statue, venerable presidents, is the fruit of toil, to be awarded by the purest judgment, so that its splendour may befit both parties: it should neither disfigure the recipient by coming from an unworthy giver, nor stain the giver by being conferred on one who does not deserve it. If the voice of one who loathes vice is free to speak against a tyrant, if faults may be pressed home even under a protector of crimes, I will say what I think. An honourable thing has fluttered between two wicked men and, protected by neither, has known neither from whom it came nor to whom it passed. Consider into whose hands a thing long decreed for the brave, and to be won at the price of blood, has fallen: a usurper of power bestows it, and the slayer of a father receives it. I do not know where to turn. Caught among the precipices of your virtues, venerable prince, I do not know whether to accuse you for being a tyrant or for honouring parricides with a reward. You both deserve the cross, and to be driven out of this present life in the sack. Do you not think it enough to have escaped the punishment you deserve, unless you also bestow what is not lawful and he receives what he does not deserve? You presumed these things through your audacity long ago, when you broke into the citadel of justice as its destroyer, raised to dominion by the same kind of merits for which you have now given another a statue. Inevitably, most eminent men, all people cherish what they have themselves been, and excesses are not usefully corrected except by those who have reformed. He has a shameless face who believes that one who follows crime will punish evil. A judge's conscience is bound by the need to keep its secret, and does not think itself free to condemn in its subjects what it did not hesitate to commit itself. By what successes, or by what varied steps, did you arrive at this, you sewer of crimes, that once you had risen to the heights you were allowed to sin so greatly, whenever you wished, as to invite the disgraceful to higher honours with statues? You have exchanged the taste of liberty for the gall of slavery; he turned the obedience owed to his father into swords. Consider how praiseworthy are the things you have injured, and, without the accuser saying a word, judge what a father and freedom deserve. You bind free necks to the yoke of a most wretched condition; with him the law of nature counted for nothing. What you do to your fatherland, he did to his parent. In this respect you should perhaps be thought the crueller, because you administer harsh commands under a kind of living death, and do not grant an end, as if with a healing hand, to those for whom death is desirable. He, unwilling to let his begetter remain in the world, snatched life with a deadly blow from the author of his light. I do not know by what difference of crimes they are to be distinguished; meanwhile, if it is permitted, they should be joined in punishment. If the swelling of some arrogance had lifted you up above your fellow citizens, the injured community would have marked you out as a defendant, and your immoderate elevation would have proclaimed you a forswearer of the sweetness of private life. If he had so much as looked on his begetter with a grim stare while his father was unharmed, he would have earned the guilt of a parricide. See, then, what is fitting for these men, who have reached the very summit of offences. There is nothing left that either the afflicted fatherland or the slain father can believe remains to be done. Far be it from us, leading men, to aggravate the offence with arguments. The bare names of the defendants are enough, and they are to be protected by no privilege of defence. I will, however, add to the charge certain things that are the very height of guilt, so that nothing may seem to have been withheld from the case which you, I judge, have tracked down with keen scent. The parricide's statue is surrounded and fenced in by the brave on either side, and the likenesses that either the care of letters produced or the Field of Mars cast in bronze are ranked below his image. Believe me, so many heroes take it hard that by no inscriptions and by no reward are they distinguished from the shedder of a father's blood, and if any vigour remains in their souls, they lament their rewards, which they won by the exertion of their strength. Where is honour, where is the value of liberal study, where is the reward of one who fights for his fatherland, if a usurper sets up bronze figures in the public squares and the man who brought about his father's death obtains them? Only impose torments worthy of their deserts, lest, if an unequal penalty condemns the accused, the praise for judging rightly should not be owed to you either. Let those whose share in the offence has proved almost equal be driven from life by one and the same road.
XIX. A declamation given to Ambrose, against a gambler who staked as the price of a game the field in which his parents were buried.

Judges, after this man had been brought down to a meagre fortune by the shameful pursuit of gambling, and the failure of his means had handed him over to an ever-growing passion for play, then even his parents' tombs began to be no longer kept back from a shameful stake. Then the uncertain throws of chance began to be awaited over ashes, and laughable moments of contest were set over tears. Where are those who say that souls which have finished with the light have nothing in common with the inhabitants of this world, and that once separated from the world the departed have their own day? See, this man's ancestors have almost grown old together with the tombs they had obtained, and through long ages the very barrows now need burying; and yet, in the eyes of this most shameless reveller, they are still thought to have kept their value as stakes in a contest. After the long course of their lives, shades who owe nothing to chance are ordered to await their fate from the dice. After squandering the wealth your parents gathered by long thrift, after the many pounds of silver and gold that frugality kept under careful measure to help an heir, you, offspring worse than childlessness, have honoured the urns of your forebears by making them stakes on the gaming board. If a lesser care on the part of posterity adorned the mausoleums of those who went before, the negligence would deserve punishment, and would look for its penalty from those judges who wish to correct their own sons' morals in the offences of others. But you, instead of the festival returning by the fixed law of the seasons, instead of garlands and the offerings on which souls are fed, thought it wrong if your parents' tombs did not change owners. You would not have been allowed to sell these final dwellings even to ransom your own child carried off by enemies. I ask what necessity there is that I see a stranger as owner among your parents' ashes, and nothing else is put to me but a game. O wretched condition of mortals, both when their desires are denied and when they are granted to their greater misfortune! How often did your parents move God with anxious sighs that they might not pass from the enjoyment of this light without a lawful heir, which is thought the most ill-omened fate of all? How often did a mind ignorant of the future come close to death at the pallor of their child? Born, brought up, educated, he has come to this harvest, judges, with a mind starved of shame: after losing everything, he does not allow those who gave him his patrimony to remain even in their own place. We condemn in this criminal his most shameful intent; for perhaps it may happen that by a stroke of kindly fortune you have released your forebears' bones to decent masters. Reverence for the dead is common to all, and all humanity demands fitting worship for the sanctity of those laid to rest by the final lot. Yet the last rites are paid more excellently to our own ancestors, whom veneration so sets before our eyes that we believe the carrying out of the instructions of the dead to be an offering made to the gods. We observe everything they have commanded, not believing that anything violated of their precepts goes unpunished. I find no new manner of speech with which to set forth this new kind of crime. If it was sacrilege not to obey them, what is it to have sold their final dwellings for a game? Believe, judges, that all this man's forefathers stand before your eyes awaiting the hour of vengeance. If they are appeased, care for parents may be confirmed without stain to endure for posterity.
XX. A declamation against a man who placed a statue of Minerva in a brothel.

We believe that the verdict of venerable judges has always been uncertain when the sin is confused. The judge's deliberation has hesitated over which way to incline where the nature of the offence was doubtful; for just as manifest vices demand a verdict in keeping with equity, so obscure ones hold it in suspense. But when the crime is in plain view, what hope remains for the one to be condemned? Take this into your minds, I beg you, and weigh with inward judgment what sort of man this is, who has violated both the eyes of virginity and the secrets of the brothel. Sacrilegious on both counts, he neither respects the vices, to which he has brought a hostile witness, nor spares the blush of chastity, which he joins to unworthy company. I demand of you, monster of the human race, what religious devotion led your frivolity to set up a statue of Minerva, when the insult inflicted by the foulness of the place shows you to be an enemy of purity; and the public corruption cries out that you show no reverence for the defilements of Venus either. Those who are spurred to transgression by love of excess know no limits to sin; those who have plotted towering crimes know no measure in their errors. While, in mockery, you join into one by your craft Dione and Pallas, the most opposite of deities, given over to the beliefs of strangers, you have made your offence harsher by your very religion. It is a deed deserving the gravest expiation to mix things that are at odds and gather into one those whom you insult unless you keep them apart. Do you believe a man can be found who holds to neither of this world's two ways of life, and is neither a friend to the virtues nor found faithful to the vices? The patronage of faults often leads some to despise good works, and those who are strangers to the taste of praise rejoice in the fruits of licence. But which of these two ways will find you its follower? You have laid hostile hands on the better order, and you do not even bow your neck in sincere obedience to the wicked. I hate, leading men, those who judge their own conduct laxly; I condemn those who through neglect of upright actions fall under suspicion. Yet even more do I detest those who, caught in both camps, show a steady conscience to neither. For those whom you see keeping faith with their sins promise, when the time of repentance comes, devotion to virtue. If, most wicked of men, the thought of Minerva had stirred you when you stood before the shrine of Venus, would the memory in your mind, loving both powers so badly, have wronged them both? You would have fled the dwelling of the goddess whose adversary you were holding in your mind. What honour is it to have set her statue in a place where the goddess of chastity could be violated merely by being mentioned there? By not knowing, most ill-starred man, how to climb by degrees to the summit of accursed error, you have all but stirred up war again among the heavenly beings. Those eyes of hers are forever seeing foul things, eyes that loathe embraces joined by some law of obscenity. While through your management a captive deity attends the brothels, you alone have shown that the power of the gods above serves human lust, and that they are bound to whatever places mortals have assigned them. How discordant will be the outlay on burnt sacrifices! The offering made to one deity will insult the other. For since, by your foresight, a twofold divine power occupies a single couch, and modesty and wantonness meet in one temple, neither goddess will look with favour on our devotion: those whom you have mixed together in one dwelling we shall find offended by their own sacrifices. What sort of gifts will they be that must be carried in throngs by unchaste women and virgins alike? One goddess is to be offended by merriment, and the other appeased by wantonness. Amid the sacred boughs and the incense, the victims will be a cause of strife, and the deities will be angered by the very means by which they are soothed. I spare these sacrileges a lengthy narration. Let the defendant use up among his punishments the delays he would otherwise enjoy in the light of life, since the foulness even of another's deeds disfigures the one who recounts them.
XXI. A declamation [against a certain father who, although he did not deign to ransom his son when he was captured by a pirate, nevertheless demanded to be supported by him].
THEME. LAW.

Children must either support their parents or be put in chains. A certain man had two sons, one frugal and one dissolute. Both fell into the hands of pirates. They wrote to their father about a ransom. The father sold his property and went to the pirates. Because he had brought too little money, he was given the choice of ransoming whichever son he wished. He chose to ransom the dissolute son, because he was ill. That son died on the way home. The frugal son escaped from the pirates. The father asks him for support. He refuses. This case is argued against Quintilian, for he defends the father and we defend the son. I ask you who read this not to think it arrogance.
PREFACE.

Is it ever right to speak against Quintilian except on behalf of the truth? Or does eagerness to speak make a man forget himself when he lends his words to justice? Polish suits deceivers, when eloquence, painted with the brush of falsehood, puts on a borrowed beauty that deserves praise only in words. Let fairness be asserted without the support of the orator's art: I choose the pageantry that honesty will bring forth once it is defended. Let plainness, protected by the favour of heaven, advance against that most eloquent man; our daring springs from confidence in our cause. Only grant us your goodwill, distinguished gentlemen, while keeping your ears and minds on guard, so that the lofty tragic buskin, with the power of speech in which it excels, does not believe victory is already its own. What else is helping us against his onslaught but bringing justice home after a long exile?
OPENING.

I would rejoice, most distinguished judges, at having escaped the filth of prison and the chains of the pirates, were it not that on my return my father has taken the place of the pirate ships. He asks support from me, though he freed me from the enemy neither with gold nor with tears. He thinks that the return of the son he did not ransom when he could ought to benefit him. In vain do you beg for food by the benefit of the law, you who dissolved the rights of nature by your deeds. The law decrees that food be supplied to fathers, but that sacred bond does not lie in the name alone. Let even the pirate say whether you are a father. You often say that I was better than the son who died, but you never showed it when you made your judgement. Consider the course of my late brother's faults: the son who was preferred was more like his father in character. With what omen I have spent my life in conduct quite foreign to theirs became plain when my father willingly abandoned me to the brigands. He thinks he puts forward strong arguments against his offspring when he boasts that the guilty son, already close to the grave, deserved greater favour. I beg you, judges, declare what I owe. Meanwhile it is clear that I was ranked even below the ashes of a vicious man. He does not blush to demand anything by a parent's authority from one toward whom he refused to be what he is called. If only the pirates' chains had preserved my health for such uses! I would make my father a captive of shame by supplying food I do not owe, so that the unjust judge would groan at the injustice of his own sentence. For food supplied by someone to whom you have done no good drains you: the stomach goes hungry in its very fullness when it has no awareness of a kindness given beforehand. I do not know what remnant of hope that man thinks he has from his two sons, when he gave one back to the earth and allowed the other to be kept under the perpetual rule of robbers. Let him take, if he is not ashamed, whatever limbs exhausted by torture can earn. I do not know what an old man demands from a cripple; meanwhile, as I see it, we both need feeding. Why do you bring up to me the excuse of your modest means? A man who wanted to ransom only one son sold his property in such a way that the price would not suffice for both. Who could describe my misfortune, who my miseries? After the Cilicians, even the freedom I have regained is said to be in bondage. Tell me, judges, I pray: if even in my own country I am to be declared a debtor, what have I escaped? My most saintly begetter has added that I am grieved that the chains released my brother. As if nature demanded so much servitude of us that joy at a brother's rescue should make up for my being left behind! We owe love to our kin when we ourselves are free. Believe one who speaks plain truths: joy over another cannot enter a man who fears for himself. For he cries out, in the manner of a dishonest argument, that the one from whom something is asked is somehow the richer. Painted refinement keeps this trick for its entreaties: it uses a contrived humility as darts, so that, with the cement of a proud self-abasement, it leaves nothing free to the one who is asked. He testifies that his fortune was bid for both sons, though it is agreed that it was spent for one: he expects double gratitude for a single favour. I do not know whether we should ask what he intended, when it is clear to everyone what he did. The pirate exhausted every defence on your side when he gave you the choice between us. Let the father who ransomed only the son who was going to die keep the one thing he wanted from a son: a tomb. For he who preferred the sick son to the healthy one declared that he shrank from the son who would live. What you seek from the survivor I do not know, since you have for your consolation the tears you bought.
STATEMENT OF FACTS.

Judges, I have always cultivated decency, even at an age friendly to sin, and I withheld spending from boyish desires so that my mature years might have something to enjoy. Through my thrift in this I made sure that my father had something left to offer for his dissolute son. Why do you complain of the meagreness of the estate? Had I been like him in character, things would have come to such a pass that neither of us could have been ransomed. He is an unfair judge who wanted another to profit from what I had built up by my self-restraint. To judge by my father's severity, my honesty was the cause of my long captivity. Healthy, diligent, attentive to father and brother: such a son does not deserve to be brought back to his homeland. And had we not been taken captive by one and the same lot, my return would have been tarnished by suspicion. We were equal in calamity, but far apart in our father's love. Fortunate young man! Thanks to the support of his extravagance he both used up a large part of the common estate beforehand and profited from what was left. Wretched me, always a captive by my father's verdict! In peacetime I rehearsed what I would later endure, and while I kept to the path of right, the practice of thrift taught me how one lives among enemies. That is why I lived content with the food those savages provided, finding in my extremity comfort in habit, not in any humanity of the robber. I ask: for whom did that more frugal way of life preserve me, if regard for what is right earns the displeasure of fathers?
OBJECTION.

What of his claim that the barbarian said, "You have brought the price of only one"? Objections always receive the reply they deserve. You were not anxious about any bidding: before anyone had pleaded, you displayed the gold you had brought before the enemies' eyes. Since everything went your way like this, no one could doubt that the release of one son was enough for your wishes. And as soon as you entered those caves filled with the squalor of death, the pirate knew whom you would choose before he gave you the choice. That trepidation did not come from love: he leaves nothing in doubt who, by every sign of affection, speaks about his two sons as if he had come for one. After your departure stricter guards confined me. Thanks be to the deity if it protected my freedom in this as well, that I escaped. Meanwhile your decision seems to have sent the enemy this message: "Unless the one I leave behind is carefully guarded, he will slip away." With the gods as our guides, our flight succeeded even under the enemies' eyes.
DIGRESSION.

Moreover, my father is rich in speech, and long life has taught him to make vivid what he says and to impose necessity on minds through the ear. He says that food is common to all who share in humanity, and he demands from one person what no one may refuse, alleging in general that whatever the earth produces is owed to everyone. But back when the cornfields poured out their wheaten offspring and the vineyards their liquor for common use, and the land had not yet been divided among farmers man by man, no one left his son among enemies in such a way that he would be thought to have preferred mourning to that son's slavery. I do not know, judges, what he seeks from the survivor after he chose tears. But he throws the fear of the law in our face, and he wants what is written about parents and children to be owed to him, though he showed nothing of a parent. He seeks our goodwill while we are being compelled. He wants us to offer to filial devotion what he himself has declared no one can refuse, whatever excuse he makes, because he is afraid. Is there room for mercy where command presses? What may not be withheld cannot be said to be given generously. Clemency does not deserve the name unless it is freely given. Whatever you have the power not to give, count as a sincere gift, if you give it. But the constant repetition of "nature" and the sacred name of "begetter" will be set against us, as if the enjoyment of light, a gift obtained from the heavenly powers, could be counted among the things that human beings bestow. It is sacrilege to call the bounty of the gods the seed of mortals. A cruel father can testify only to his lust. He even adds to my burdens when he demands the comforts due to the destitute, saying that the city could have helped him if I had not returned. What else does that wish reveal but that the pirate should take me again? If the sight of your unransomed offspring is a burden to you, then surely you shall possess, at no price, what you usually buy at great cost: my tomb. My age indeed promises life, but the severity of the torments, which I endured more bitterly after you left, promises death.
EXAMPLES.

Next you brought forward examples worthy of a father's purpose, but your interpretation cheapened them, as if antiquity had supplied a pattern for your desires rather than models of holy conduct to imitate. What weight did the shoulders of great Aeneas feel from his father's burden? Or did Anchises weigh down with his body the son whom he himself had often carried by his conduct? Do you want to know why he deserved to be rescued from the enemy? It is set before our eyes that he did not want it, for fear of being a burden. He believed that the ruin of falling Ilium gave him a burial, and so that his aged limbs would not hold back his departing son, who was more worthy of life, he said the fall of the city was tomb enough for him. He was willing to stay behind so that his son could escape the brigands; you returned to your homeland and left your son behind. Why do you recall the noble deeds of Scipio on behalf of his father? When he devotedly offered himself for his parent, he gave everything, yet he did not use up all that he owed. Good wishes always arise from like causes, and acts of kindness do not go only one way. A man who reckons that his son will not come to the duties of nature unless forced declares what he deserves from that son. The law threatens chains unless I obey. What does it matter? The long years of punishment that you arranged for me have trained me to this habit, although long endurance of penalties does not make a man defiant. Yet I wonder whether my father has inflicted on me what I escaped from the barbarians. There is no point in escaping brigands if the same lot follows you home. As far as I can see, the hardship of one's native soil and of a foreign land is one and the same, and the bitterness is no different for those who return and those held captive. Indeed I find no difference at all, nor do I ask which chain in particular shall bind my neck: whether I am bound with links of stiff iron or pay a tax to a gullet, the condition is the same. Hungry, I shall carry feasts to a man who is well fed and, what is worse, does not love me. With what disdain will he throw away the food I offer? With what rancour will he trample on my devotion? He is a man I could not find merciful even when I was in my extremity. He declares that he learned from our letters of the ransom sought equally for me and my brother [?], that we begged for release with equal tears, that we wrote our letters in the same plight. I do not deny it; I do not refute it: he wins on this objection. But this I demand to know: what caused one son to receive what was owed to two, since two had asked? You went to sea for both of us and, as you claim, crossed the threats of the watery element with devotion as your guide. Who would believe in a twofold love from a man who came back with one son? Mercy is never praised unless it has been put to the test: how can anyone without shame proclaim his affection when it produced no effect? Does the key of speech always truly unlock the secret of the heart? Devotion that is not also held fast, silently, in deeds is mere show. Love will stand with unshaken roots among all men, if boasting [?] is enough. The law says: "Let him either support or be chained"; the father cries: "This support is owed to a parent even if he does not ransom." You armed yourself for this role at the very time you were failing in the duty to which nature bound you. What was shamefully denied to innocent nature now profits an empty defence. Believe me, when the law spoke of a parent, it did not keep silent about a redeemer: it urged, commanded and compelled that all the sacred obligations of the dutiful office be fully discharged through the names themselves. My calamity clouds your mind so that you cannot understand this: the ransoming of a son, which belongs to the devotion of kinship, did not need to be in the precepts as well. You accuse me of impiety and of envy at my brother's release while you praise the children of Leda. You do not realize that if your way of sharing out had been applied between them, it would have produced a distortion: you would have condemned one to perpetual splendour of light and the other to the continual possession of night. I am lying if your judgements about your sons were any different. What did you think would happen when the pirate let go one son whom he would never have, and kept the other as if he would never release him, as though his father were handing him over? Whatever I endured in that deadly land after you were out of sight, I have no doubt came from you. All my hope was spent once the redeemer left barbarian soil without me. What ship heading for those inhuman shores did I not spot first? And whatever my eyes could not follow as the sight faded, I grasped with my mind, since those who wait most eagerly see most keenly. How often before your arrival, whenever the pirate let us look at the open air, did my father appear to me in the persons of strangers, and I saw those likenesses that love paints for itself without the disgrace of lying! Hearts long troubled are struck by such images. Alas! How often, when I refused the food the pirate provided, the barbarian comforted me with these words: "Fear nothing, do not sigh over this affliction: if your father is alive, you are not far from the haven of freedom." At last, behold, fortune answered my wishes: even the brigand eagerly announced that man's arrival to me. He who joyfully welcomed the redeemer was not far from the love of complete clemency. We did not have inhuman masters, judges: they were men who could have been softened even by prayer. If tears had made up for the lack of gold, he would have brought both of us back at once. He has shown that he did not want what he did not beg for with great effort. Weigh, I ask you, what he can rightly demand of me, when he did not help me in my extremity even with a plea. You added that you are protected by the privileges of nature, and that the wrong you did me may not be punished. But a man who rests his defence on his rank does not have the prerogative of innocence. Let the innocent shine in the light of his deeds. A man who thinks his protection lies in his precedence confesses his crimes without pretence. No authority defends the guilty; among criminals the sacred bonds of names vanish.
EPILOGUE.

Most holy judges, I have argued this after my imprisonment by robbers, with fresh toil of heart, as if, even were I not a debtor, I had the strength to provide what is demanded. He does not consider my bones stripped of flesh and fouled by the inhumanity of my masters, and he has no regard for the hidden parts of nature that the torturers laid open. Torments brought into the light whatever a man is made of in my body, and the inmost parts of my entrails were laid bare as the barbarian pressed on with his tortures, while my father disdained to stand by me. Cruelty passes all measure when, even in exacting debts, it does not first ask about strength. You see the vigour of youth in me weakened by the burden of miseries, and the strength of my years worn down by many kinds of calamity; you see that I have both the needs of old age and the resentment that youth arouses. Yet you do not stop demanding from me what even an enemy would have excused in a man so exhausted. You will receive a tributary's payment, and still you assail me with the grandeur of your title and the sacred spirit of a parent, though you disdain to show even your own child the compassion you owe to any human being. May heaven's dispensation reward your purpose with this: may you once more look upon the funerals of your offspring that you longed for, and may you, who are burdened by a living presence, take the sum of your desires from tombs.
SPEECH XXII.
PREFACE.

The excellent young man has indeed, in setting the riches of his inventions in order, endowed them abundantly with a wealth of words as well, and what he believed to be in the cause of religion he has brought forth with fitting and reverent speech. But let the inventions of malicious treatises cease, far from the snares of mere opinion. We do not set the breast of our own eloquence against Arator, nor do we cut down with a hostile pruning-hook the shoot of praise as it bursts into the light. Rather, by showing him which path of words he ought to follow, we know that we shall triumph the more brightly in him if he should happen to be preferred to us, because whatever he has generously poured out from the wealth of his learning, with God's increase, he drew from our store.
THEME. THE LAW.
From a captured enemy city, let the priests and the Vestal virgins be released as free persons.

After the successful outcome of a contest of war, amid triumphs and laurels, a law read out to the victors to restrain them can have no force. What have we accomplished with our swords in our readiness to die, if after the battles there is still something for us to fear? Whatever threatened us until now lies lifeless before my eyes, and now that the hostile host has been routed, I do not know what terror the decrees of dead princes can bring us. He does not know how to weigh the worth of proven valour who prides himself on bridling armed men with documents. Let sluggish hearts submit to such bars: I have scattered with the sword whatever took my freedom from me. The only thing anyone can deny us is what we do not want; I am content to keep within that limit which my desires have never summoned me to cross. The law grants me possession of whatever I have overcome. Let leisure and the toga gain what they can by refusing: for me, nature has brought forth all that I have wrested from the enemy while standing in battle array. The only written law we have is this: fear nothing. And these things I have put to your ears as though the formula set against us were a good one. Yet law, the nurse of brave men, the avenger of liberty, the bulwark of the fatherland, bids its heroes, once the battle is over, look again to their reward; whereas this law, not content with deeds happily achieved, takes away the wages of sweat and so breaks the zeal for fighting. Are those precepts good, then, which stand in the way of our becoming good? Whatever takes away the fruit of our labours, most prudent censors, chastises us at the expense of what belongs to others. Is it fair that sanctions drawn up from a foreign law should have force? Or does it seem anywhere near reasonable to cut off the hope of future possession? Why do you set against us the name of religion in the persons of priests? It was under the leadership of the god whom you revere in them that I won. Know that the very men you wish to escape the yoke of our servitude for his sake are held captive at his own command. He fights against the gods who raises up anyone whom their verdict has laid low: those you hurry to rescue would never have become the property of men if they had deserved to be ministers of the heavenly ones. See, I am arguing with you about the flavour of the law as though I had no weapons to hurl by way of reply. What justice do you find in that command which, in order to prop up the enemy, condemns the allies who have extended the empire? Take away the hope of plunder, and you have taken away the desire for battle. And if the spirit of the laurelled man is defrauded, whatever I sought in contempt of life will turn to regret. Let prudent men be far from seeking equity in something of this kind, which I will not call a law but a tyrant's decree, displeasing to the gods, hostile to valour, fighting against right and justice under the false colour of piety. You do not know, most talkative of men, how just a grief is born from the loss of the fruit of one's labour. This is as much as to say: whatever you have acquired with the gods as your leaders, we snatch away. I saw the enemy city grow old, as it were, in a single fire, and the very seats of the heavenly ones deserted, stripped of their divinity, and thrown down; and do you think anything remained that ought not to belong to the victor? What of the fact that this trifling and empty enactment is muddled by obscurity? For it says that priests or Vestal virgins ought to enjoy liberty. I suppose it means those in whom the dweller in heaven has shown that he has his abode, whom heavenly favour has marked with its light as greater than men. The pontiffs proclaim reverence for those whom the divine powers wish to be recognized. We saw the wretches whom [?] protects, among the ashes of the fallen city, looking for protection from lamentation alone and, having no confidence in their calling, wandering among the crowds crushed by captivity. There was no unearthly splendour in their faces, no cheerfulness to announce their office. Those who in the storms of this world find a harbour in an innocent conscience do not know how to be troubled amid adversity. We saw them more afflicted than all the others who trembled, these men to whom you grant bare names and a laughable law. What place is left for merit, if this sacred office consists in a title alone? I believe it is one thing to be called [?], another to be a pontiff. I have often seen weapons aimed at the throat fall before faces worn by fasting, and swords blunted by unarmed men lose their stiffness. If you will believe one who is about to speak of religion: he who in any danger needs human help was no minister of temples. The supreme Judge knows how to clothe his own possession with light. That heavenly admixture is not hidden, and though it be clothed in the tunic of human frailty, it flashes forth. What of the fact that they themselves come ready to serve, men who do not deserve to be dragged into servitude? He who is unworthy does not rebel at this last extremity. Those whose mind is worthy of high places run to render obedience, and those whom it is wrong to bind to dishonourable things cast off the stubbornness of mortality. These men of yours, if they by no means deserve to be released, bring dangers upon us. Those cannot be withdrawn from men's possession whom we perceive to have nothing more than a man has. Help me, comrades, help me, partners, and with the aid of truth silence the chatter of my opponent. The matter at issue is one on which we already know what the verdict of the gods has been. Let the undeserving be handed over, so that we may have good priests. In their stead let those be appointed whom no conciliating tale, no uncertain defence, but the very brightness of the supreme god proclaims to be his own.
XXIII. SPEECH [AGAINST A DISOWNED SON WHO, HAVING KILLED HIS FATHER, WAS ALSO PLOTTING AGAINST HIS MOTHER].

Judges: after the disowned son, in carrying out what he calls a just grief, avenged with the sword his father's act and his mother's consent, he thinks he can unsettle the innocence of those hearing the case and steal some acquittal for a manifest crime. We do not know what words of recommendation the criminal may find in his own defence; to refute him, we show the wound. A son ruined by wicked persistence [?], after killing his father, strives to destroy his mother's good name: grieving that we escaped his dagger, he pursues with a weapon our reputation, for which, out of the modesty of our sex, we fear the more. We show the father's severed neck; we show the path the criminal took. He arranges words against the facts, and [?] so that he might seem to have found a trustworthy support, he has drawn our little one over to his view, and, the boy knowing nothing of deceit, he has corrupted him with a contrived art of words, causing him too to perish, the one who was thought to be left to us. Why do you wish to veil naked justice with tricks? You could not spare the man you hated, nor could you have struck the one you falsely claim to have loved. Is there any need of arguments where truth bears witness to its deed with its own voice? You lost all hope of defence when you were marking your mother's limbs with the sword. But though your advocate be handsome and polished, we have no eyes for looking at such things.
XXIV. EXTEMPORE SPEECH, WHICH DEUTERIUS HIMSELF SET.
Diomedes, his sea-voyage done, safe now on dry land,
Weeps for a shipwreck suffered with no water at hand.
She for whose sake he had striven and conquered many a tide,
His wife, had gone over to be another's bride.
Though the name is feigned, the cause of his complaint is true.
Attend to his words, I pray, with kindly favour.
ADDRESS.

O gods, if not everything turns out as you dispose it, your power is divided; or else you are the authors of evils. But if care for human affairs troubles any one of your number, grant me either the happiness of a man returning home or the wandering which you, ungrateful ones, have brought to an end. If heaven is to be called the possession of the pious, if what mortals pray for is granted them for the sake of moments of joy, do not join vengeance to your benefits. Why did we press our prayers so hard toward their fulfilment? So that, by the vote of the heavenly ones, adversity might be prepared out of an occasion of prosperity? Give me back, I beg you, kindly ones, the hardships you took away: let the sea be restored to me, lest my reputation perish in a shipwreck on land. The next best thing to good fortune is not to know whatever evils have befallen. The disgrace that has struck me in the face would not have touched me while I was away. My wife (oh, the shame of it!) I would not be thought to have lost had I not come back to her: the calamity I had forsworn has overturned my state. The wandering of the liquid element was nearer to a harbour: on my native soil I have lost the port that I often found in the bays of the vast deep. Is this the home I longed for, the longing for which promised forgetfulness of dangers, when, in the hope of the joy to come, the present shape of greater ills could remain unknown? [?] To whom were beginnings ever born from the ends of miseries, or has a fresh start ever come from misfortunes already endured? Has it ever happened that what was longed for was not loved? Or that escape from danger did a man harm? Fortune has always struck me with new blows, each worse than the last: if its changes tend to the worse, let it keep to a single form of harm, lest it grow insolent through a succession of them. Companions in my misfortunes, I had a wife sent forth into chastity by the light of nature, whose splendour of birth had grown through her upbringing, so that, defended by a twofold bulwark, she could never be thought liable to the assaults of wrongdoing, nor to soften the hardness of chastity by [?] obscenity. She never sought the tawny adornment of gold, nor imitated the snow of her body with the whiteness of precious stones; she had no aids to beauty for as long as she pleased me. She knew that the rights of the marriage bond are not helped by painted pursuits, and that a wife does not keep her husband bound when she seeks any other brilliance than that which comes from character. The service of bringing up the children left her free, while she showed herself such as deserved to be longed for, and such as never thought her husband absent. She had hardened her sex by firmness of mind, while in her a woman's weak counsels took on substance from a man's authority. She was already resisting the lapses of her own kind with the healing of good teaching, and laughed at the excesses of women turned to other uses. In short, she was such a woman, when she was lost, as husbands are wont to weep for. By a Circean cup, as they say, she was changed from herself and passed over to the desire of an adulterer. But what are we to do, caught as we are amid anxieties and uncertainties? Let the hated voyage take us in as a remedy, and let hands wearied by the rigging once more take up the bonds of hemp; let my right hand cling to the tiller, to govern by the rudder the laws of the reined-in stern; let the star-painted sky be restored to my sight; let the routes of our plan be guided by the signs of the night. Let it be a solace to my eyes not to see the land of my profaned marriage: let us flee the fatherland in which our marriage has been made such that it shames us to have lost it, nor would our wishes dare to take it back.
XXV. SPEECH. WORDS OF THETIS WHEN SHE SAW ACHILLES DEAD.

A mother's deception, devised with loving counsel, has been cut short. The fates found our Achilles even though he had been stolen away into another nature, and it did no good that cunning changed the sex his birth had given him: in all that time he did not learn to be a woman, and soft habits preserved the spirit of a brave man. Who would believe that a precaution could fail which was devised by one who was both goddess and mother? Immortality is no prize when a mother cannot pass it on to her offspring, nor can it help her steal her son away from misfortune. Are we gods only so that we may never be spared from sorrow? What sort of condition is this, when from the inmost depths of our womb we bring forth what is bound to serve death? The power of the heavenly ones ought either to be allowed to confer on its posterity what it possesses, or else, when our dear ones fall, we ought to be granted death as the end of our lamenting. We are lower than men, for we bear children like them, and in this respect we lie under a worse mockery of the Fates: that we do not know death, though we are bound to it through our children. Greatest of the gods, either withdraw our offspring from the power of chance, or subject us to it as a favour. Let it be allowed us, if we cannot prevail, at least to suffer death for one we love. Bereavement stands before my eyes, the worse because, in the loftiness of my eternity, I foresaw it. O lamentable happiness of the gods, when they are not granted to avert that which, among adversities, they are not permitted not to know! I recall the anxiety of time past, and I remember the cares over which I kept watch in vain. What good was it to arm my son's body with the help of the Stygian marsh, when we sought from the waters what he ought to have received from us? In the limbs of our offspring, where the goddess held him, there is a place for a wound. Why did the water not mingle with looser fingers, so that the wave, mightier than the gods, might have kept out blows altogether? What use was it, too, to choose Chiron as his teacher, to steady the slippery years of youth with learning? By various paths of instruction, I suppose, we brought it about that war would please my son: at the hands of the bravest of counsellors it came about that the strength that followed had no wisdom to guide it. Who would want a man who has drunk in the taste of combat to be hidden among the secret quarters of women, and so provide for his child by the very means that destroys what he provides for? We were already breaking to the wool-basket hands hardened by spears, and a robe set off with gold or purple enclosed those shoulders which the hides of slain lions had warmed. It was no easy change for our young man, after a taste of glory, to imitate a girl; nor is anything skilfully contrived which I did not command in the first beginnings of his tender age. But why do I go over what is past, when the enormity of the calamity to come beats upon my mind? I see the destruction of smoking Troy, overthrown while still standing; I see the battles of Hector, bitter to the Greeks, who grew great in fame only so that, when he fell, the triumph of my son might grow in value; I see his body dragged by the four-horse chariot, as though still ready to fight, and I see that whatever is taken from the dignity of the dead is taken from the credit of my Achilles; I see that what serves his anger is lost to his gain. But why do I feed on these praises, I who am to be bereaved? The rest I will cover with silence, lest I be undone by the telling before the time of grief has come. Let our eternity have from silence the consolation which it does not have from nature.
XXVI. SPEECH. WORDS OF MENELAUS WHEN HE SAW TROY BURNED.

Although the ravisher set my grief ablaze with heavy fires, although we have endured the torches of injury, in due time the author of an immense crime has wasted away on a pyre together with the whole city bound up with him. An insult is almost a happy thing when it earns such vengeance, even at the cost of the greatest toil. Who would refuse to undertake a necessity that is to end in triumph? The taste of what follows shuts out the bitterness of what went before: what we grieved over grows sweet, because those who provoked our grief now repent of it. The occasion of a woman shamefully carried off became the mother of our increase: a wife separated from us gave birth to an empire, and out of an adulterer's embraces she bore for us the country we now hold. Let those who laughed at the man left without a wife see him treading on the proud necks of his enemies. We had a wife long schooled in honourable ways, ignorant of any other's company, who would not wish to desire what is not permitted. Habit did not hurl her headlong into vice; it was by the pressure of a wicked robber that she followed Paris with a captive will. Awareness of her beauty never led her to think she was adored, because, as we firmly believe, those women are most shameful in character who remember that they are beautiful. Such vengeance befitted one who had sinned so greatly: he who seized the height of a revered wife has fallen utterly. Enjoy such a wedding as this, adulterer. Alecto follows you as bridesmaid with these insignia, and [?]. So it was fitting that Paris too should perish thus. We have laid down the laws of marriage not with speech but with swords, laying waste the crop of presumption with an avenging sickle. Our losing a marriage will help many to preserve theirs. Tell me, you women who anywhere have received the name of wife: whenever vices creep up on you, will not the name and the valour of Menelaus come to mind? For those to whom chastity is not a matter of desire, it will be, unless we are mistaken, a matter of necessity: the same discipline will be kept by all, when both the willing and the compelled keep to one pattern.
XXVII. SPEECH. WORDS OF JUNO WHEN SHE SAW THAT ANTAEUS HAD PROVED EQUAL IN STRENGTH TO HERCULES.

At last, at long last, someone has been found to answer to our purpose, someone who would triumph over our enemy even while being defeated. The strength of Hercules will not lie down unless it crushes its foe; but the one we have provided grows proud even of his falls. He stands great in his own strength, but he will be greatest through his overthrow. I do not know whether Hercules can be his equal, or whether Antaeus cannot by any means be laid low; but if adversity flatters our enemy, we come to the laurels. We know the future, but it befits the gods to speak to mortals in human fashion. Let Hercules consider what course he chooses to take. He is bound to be beaten if his enemy engages him, and bound to be beaten if his enemy lies down. He who made sport of poisons in the cradle, who brought peace to the groves of Erymanthus, who outran the hind in speed, let him have the choice of what to do: either he will throw his enemy and perish, or, if he fears the contest, he will already be buried with his own rocks. The peril of Lerna, unless I am mistaken, will spring up again from the very completion of the contest. Who would not believe that nothing remains to be done once the enemy is seen stretched on the ground? But the effort of our side will be roused by being crushed, and the deed, seemingly accomplished happily against the enemy, will supply the cause for increasing his strength.
XXVIII. SPEECH. [WORDS OF DIDO WHEN SHE SAW AENEAS DEPARTING.]
No goddess was your mother, nor was Dardanus the founder of your race.

As your harshness shows, you have lost the proof of your lineage, which you falsely claim by repute. It is plain that one who loves nothing is not the son of Venus. It is the order of things that character declares descent, and that each follows the ways of the parent through whom he came into the light. The goddess of Idalium does not acknowledge one who does not know how to repay kindness. It is not fame that shows who are sons, but likeness of conduct: if the disposition is different, one who is called offspring can hardly be believed to be so. Rather, the crags of the harsh Caucasus bore you, or a rocky womb poured you forth, conceived in the recesses of the mountains, and, lest your dreadful nature be softened by nursing, Hyrcanian tigers, who rob others of life, gave you their milk: that ferocity which slaughters nursed you. For why should I make myself promises by pretending? Or why am I held in suspense by hoping for better things? He did not answer with tears the weeping I poured out, tormented by love of him; his cruel mind did not console my groans with sighs of its own. In my sorrows he did not show himself a companion of equal grief, which is the one remedy, since in distress almost the only relief is to have found someone to share it. But what

Neither the favouring eye of Juno nor the gaze of the highest Thunderer will suffer this: that in return for all I have spent I should be consumed by separation, and gain nothing by my devotion except to deserve not to be loved. Alas, faith has been driven out by all mortals, and what until now bound men to the gods has been expelled! I, pitiable woman, took in a shipwrecked man and subjected a queen to his rule, a captive though her lot of happiness remained: I made the fugitive play the lord over her who ruled. Now, inflamed with fury, I am tortured, and I groan that my master deserts me. So, summoned by the auguries of Apollo, you depart, and you prefer the chance of Lycian lots to a sure dominion already in your hands? Of course this cruelty is arranged by heavenly authors, and the interpreter of the gods drives a man to such excesses that he flees the shores of the woman who loves him as though they were hostile soil, and that he who flees only affection betrays his safety amid storms. Go: I will hold you back no longer. The road by which I am deserted holds my vengeance; the sea will pass judgment on your madness. I shall hear the hoarse surges of the swelling storms: amid the dangers you will call on the name of Dido, who was a harbour to you and gave you one. Or surely (and this I fear, lest, while I am avenged, you die while I still live) I shall learn the outcome of your longed-for voyage only after my enjoyment of the light is ended. See the undeserved wage paid for crimes: I would rather die innocent than see him die deserving it.

Hard and untamed, he boasts himself sprung from Venus' seed,
And, forswearing her, extols the goddess's line.
So Venus bore a son who flees the very name of love,
And her gentleness has poured out the venom of a raging heart.
